en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Guang. Chapter One:
Analysis of the Elements (Dhātu-paryāya). Part One of the First.
Regarding the explanation of this treatise, there is a threefold analysis: first, clarifying the origin of the treatise; second, explaining the treatise itself.
Section Three: Separate Exegesis According to the Text As for the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, it was composed by Vasubandhu.
"Vasu" means "world," and "bandhu" means "kinsman.
Thus, his name signifies "Kinsman of the World."
In India, there was a person commonly known as Vasubandhu;
because the people of the world drew near to him and made offerings to him,
he was given this name.
The parents of a bodhisattva derive their names from the place where they beg for alms.
The old translation "deva" (heaven) is erroneous.
If one speaks of "Heaven," it should be termed *deva*.
A Bodhisattva is one whose learning penetrates both the internal and external [teachings].
He was profoundly versed in the events of antiquity and the present;
his fame resounded throughout the Five Heavens,
and his reputation spread across the four quarters.
Thus, he was able to remain in obscurity for several years while investigating the source of the teachings of the *Vibhāṣā*;
then, at once composing his treatise, he spread his fragrant fame throughout the ages.
He secretly clarified the oral traditions and resolved the doubts of the Sarvāstivādins.
I pray that you will explain the text of this verse so as to dispel my lingering doubts.
This treatise has a literary style like an interlocking chain, drawing forth myriad strands;
its meaning is like a linked ring, without beginning or end.
It gathers the essential principles of the *Ṣaḍpāda-śāstra* exhaustively and without omission;

it reveals the wondrous gateways of the eight aggregates as clearly as if gazing at the palm of one’s hand. Although it expounds the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda, it occasionally corrects them according to the Sautrāntika school.
The Master of Treatises established his thesis based on reason rather than adhering to sectarian bias; consequently,
even the ninety-six heterodox schools were led to study this text together.
The eighteen heterodox schools all delighted in the secret scriptures;
they independently interpreted them, giving rise to divergent views, and thus established their various sects.
Each was said to be worth a string of cities;
all were praised as illuminating a chariot-load.
Yet this single treatise alone stands preeminent, towering and exquisite beyond compare.
It is like Mount Sumeru standing firm amidst the vast ocean, or like the brilliant sun eclipsing the multitude of stars;
therefore, the students of Indian learning call it the *Cintāmaṇi-śāstra* (The Treatise on Intelligence). Formerly, there was the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
I have already completed the translation of this treatise at Lingbiao;
however, because the local dialects were not fully integrated,
there are occasional errors and discrepancies.
As for such matters as the non-attainment of the present life, which previous sages alike have doubted,
or the fact that permanence is neither cause nor fruit, which former worthies have failed to discern—
cases such as these are difficult to explain in full detail.
To briefly cite two or three examples to illustrate this current translation:
The Upādhyāya, the Tripiṭaka Master, set his mind upon the wide propagation [of the Dharma] and vowed to travel to the Western Regions.
There, he sought out and revealed the profound scriptures, exhausting the bequeathed teachings of Vulture Peak.
He exhausted the remaining expositions of the sages within the Dharma-gate of the *Zhaoxi* (Beheading the Proclamation).
Thereafter, he traveled extensively to observe the sacred sites of the saints,
and his inquiries into the Way were thorough and complete.
Having returned to the capital and received an imperial decree to translate this treatise,
it was translated at the Great Ci'en Monastery during the Yonghui era.
The phrasing and meaning are complete and exhaustive;
the subtle principles are flawless.
In transmitting those Sanskrit words, the primary concern was to preserve their original form.
It is my hope that those whose doubts remain may see them dissolve like melting ice,
and that those who await a definitive resolution may truly forget both food and sleep.
This constitutes the first account of the origin of this elucidating treatise.
Regarding the explanation of the title:
*Abhidharma* establishes its name by way of its form; *Kośa* [is established] by way of its substance.
This indicates a specific designation for one division:
*Abhi* means "confrontation" (*prati*), because it involves the confrontation between the subject and the object; *Dharma*... [is the object].
It is called "Dharma" because it sustains and gives rise to understanding; it is called "Pitaka" (Basket) in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
"Compendium" (saṃgraha) refers to that by which [the subject] is gathered;
"treatise" (śāstra) refers to discourse, namely the instruction of disciples. Because this fascicle stands at the beginning, it is called the first.
Regarding the first chapter, "The Analysis of the Elements":
what follows is the third section, the detailed interpretation according to the text.
This section contains three parts.
First, clarifying that this treatise was composed based on the sūtras;
second, separately explaining the titles of the chapters;
third, providing the correct interpretation according to the text. Regarding the first, clarifying that this treatise was composed based on the sūtras:
In the West, all treatises are commentaries on the Buddha’s sutras.
Although the scriptural teachings are numerous,
they may be summarized into three types.
These are the three seals of the Dharma:
first, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
second, all phenomena are without self.
Third is the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
Because this seals all phenomena, it is called the "Dharma Seal.
That which accords with this seal is the Buddha’s sūtra.
If one deviates from these seals, it is not the teaching of the Buddha;
therefore, later commentators all explain the Dharma-seals (dharmamudrā), though their intentions regarding the breadth or brevity of their expositions differ.
Some provide a partial explanation of only a single Dharma-seal.
There are cases where one [topic] is raised to clarify all three;
for example, the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* and similar works explain only the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-anityatā*),
while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and similar works explain only the tranquility of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-śānti*).
This is a partial explanation of one of the Dharma-seals.
It is like the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* and other treatises which explain the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*).
This is an instance of citing one to clarify the three. The reason for explaining it in this manner is as follows:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" clarifies only the conditioned;
"nirvāṇa is tranquil" clarifies only the unconditioned;
"all dharmas are without self" clarifies both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
In order to demonstrate that this treatise encompasses all matters without exception,
it is explained in detail. Second, regarding the specific explanation of the titles of the chapters,
there are two parts within this section.
First, the correct explanation of the chapter title;
second, the clarification of the sequence of the chapters. Regarding the correct explanation of the chapter title:
it refers to the meaning of "clan" (*gotra*).
The meaning of "holding" (dhāraṇa),
the meaning of "nature" (prakṛti),
and the term "element" (dhātu); "category" (varga) refers to "classification" (prakāra).
This is the "Chapter on the Elements" (*Dhātu-nirdeśa*); thus it is named the "Chapter on the Elements.
Because this chapter explains [the subject] extensively, it is called "Analysis" (*Vibhaṅga*). In total, from beginning to end, this treatise consists of nine chapters.
This chapter stands at the beginning, hence it is called "the first.
Alternatively, it may be explained as "the first" with a numerical modifier (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*). Question: Within this chapter, the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*) are also elucidated.
For what reason is it designated by the term "dhātu"?
The explanation states:
*dhātu* means "nature" (*prakṛti*).
The term "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to essence (*svabhāva*).
This chapter elucidates the essence of all phenomena;
it is titled by means of the term "elements" (*dhātu*).
The aggregates (skandha) and bases (āyatana) are not mentioned separately because they lack substantial reality. Furthermore,
it is explained that among the three— aggregates, bases, and elements (dhātu)—
the term "element" has the broadest scope.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Although the scope of its meaning is broad,
its name is narrow and thus not mentioned here.
Furthermore, it is explained that both the names and the meanings of the aggregates (skandha) are too narrow to be taught [in full].
Moreover, the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings vary as superior, middling, and inferior.
Those of superior faculties understand when the aggregates are explained concisely.
Those of medium capacity understand only after a somewhat longer period of discernment;
those of inferior capacity awaken only when the exposition of the realms is extensive.
The superior [capacity] can encompass the lower, benefiting all three types of faculties through the realms.
The lower does not reach the upper;
they abide in two [realms] and constitute one aggregate.
Furthermore, it is named "Dhātu" because it is more extensively and excellently presented;
another interpretation holds that this chapter extensively analyzes the meaning of the eighteen *dhātus* through various categories,
and thus it is titled with the term "Dhātu."
The aggregates and sense-bases are not like that. Regarding the sequence of the two chapters on "Exposition":
this treatise consists of nine chapters in total, explaining the selflessness of all phenomena within the Buddha’s sūtras.
The first eight chapters clarify the phenomena (*dharma*) of all things;
although they also clarify principles, this is said from the perspective of the majority, as they do not primarily elucidate them.
The final chapter explains the principle of non-self (*anātman*); although it also clarifies phenomena, this is said from the perspective of the majority.

Alternatively, it is not that this is not the primary clarification; rather, because phenomena (*vastu*) are coarse, they are explained first, while principles (*yukti*) are subtle and clarified later.
Furthermore, it is explained that phenomena are the basis (*āśraya*), and for that reason, they are explained first.
Principle (*li*) is that which depends [on something else], and therefore it is explained later. Within the preceding eight chapters,
the first two chapters generally clarify the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
while the subsequent six chapters specifically clarify the contaminated and uncontaminated.
The general principle is clarified first because it serves as the basis;
the specific details are explained later because they depend upon that general explanation.
This is just as various treatises first present a general chapter and only subsequently provide detailed exegesis. Within this clarification of the general principle:
The Chapter on Elements (Dhātuvarga) elucidates the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
although it also clarifies their functions,
this is stated from the perspective of the predominant aspect.
Alternatively, it is not primarily an exposition of the nature [of phenomena].
In the "Chapter on the Faculties" (*Indriya-varga*), although the functions of all phenomena are explained, their essential natures are also clarified.
Speaking from the perspective of the majority, this is not necessarily a formal exposition. Since the essence (svabhāva) is fundamental, the elements (dhātu) are explained first;
since function arises based on essence, the faculties (indriya) are explained next. Within the detailed explanation of the six categories:
The first three chapters clarify contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Although uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are also explained therein,
they are discussed primarily from the perspective of the majority.
Alternatively, it is not exclusively the exposition of the luminous; the latter three chapters explain the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
Although tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas are also explained therein, this is stated from the perspective of the majority.
Alternatively, it is not that [the order] clearly indicates [this]; rather, contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are coarse,
and therefore they are mentioned first,
while uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are subtle.
Therefore, they are explained later.
For example, within the Four Noble Truths, suffering and its origin are explained first, followed by cessation and the path.
Furthermore, it is explained that those things with outflows are to be loathed.
Therefore, it is clarified first;
having induced weariness [with the conditioned], one causes delight [in the unconditioned].
This is why the untainted (anāsrava) is explained last. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
The outflowing (sāsrava) [factors] have arisen from beginningless time;
therefore, they are explained first.
The non-outflowing (anāsrava) [factors] are newly produced.
Therefore, it is explained later that, regarding the specific classification of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), there are three categories:
namely, the worldly (*laukika*), karma, and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
These are presented in their respective order according to the triad of fruit, cause, and condition.
The Chapter on the World explains the fruits of outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because their characteristics are coarse and easily wearying,
they are explained first.
Although causes and conditions are also explained therein, they are spoken of mostly from a general perspective and are not a formal exposition;
it is the *Karmavarga* that explains the causes for the ripening of results.
The fruit necessarily arises from its cause;
because the power of that cause is predominant,
it is explained next.
Although results and conditions are also clarified therein,
they are spoken of from a predominant perspective,
or perhaps not explicitly clarified; the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* clarifies the conditions for karma.
Karma cannot produce its fruit by itself;
it must depend upon its conditions.
The production of fruit by latent dispositions (anuśaya) is somewhat inferior to that of karma.
Therefore, it is explained later.
Although both fruit and cause are clarified therein,
it is described from the perspective of the majority.
Alternatively, this is not a general exposition; rather, within the specific exposition of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), there are three categories:
namely, the noble ones (*ārya*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, the sequence is determined by means of the three categories of fruit, cause, and condition.
The "Chapter on the Noble Ones" clarifies the untainted fruit (*anāsrava-phala*),
because its characteristics are manifest and easy to aspire toward.
Therefore, it was explained first.
Although causes and conditions are also clarified therein,
this is stated from the perspective of the predominant factor.
Alternatively, it may not be a direct explanation; rather, this section on wisdom clarifies the cause for realizing the fruit.
The fruit necessarily relies upon its cause, and furthermore, the realization of the fruit is paramount.
Therefore, it is explained next.
Although both the fruit and the conditions are also clarified therein,
this is stated from the perspective of the predominant factor.
The accomplishment [of wisdom] is not explicitly clarified here; rather, this chapter on concentration explains the conditions for wisdom.
Wisdom alone cannot realize the fruit;
it must necessarily rely upon the condition of concentration.
The power of concentration regarding that fruit is somewhat inferior;
therefore, it is explained later.
Although both fruit and cause are also clarified therein, [the former] is stated first.
This is stated from a general perspective;
it may not be a precise definition.
As for the statement "I shall explain all aspects," I will now do so.
Below this is the third section: the correct interpretation based on the text.
This treatise, as a whole, consists of three major sections: first, the introduction (nidāna); second, the main body; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the first, the introduction:
Second, the main body;
third, the dissemination.
These were composed by the Sage.
Since there must be a cause for this, the introduction (nidāna) is first elucidated.
Once the introduction has been made manifest, there must be that which is taught; therefore, the main body (saddharma) is elucidated next.

The Main Body having concluded, the Exhortation to Study and the Dissemination are explained next in order to ensure its circulation. Regarding these three divisions, there are three different interpretations.
The first interpretation states:
The first three verses of the stanzas are called the introductory section (*nidāna*).
From the words "What dharma is called... onwards, up to the Chapter on Refuting the Self (*pudgala-pratiṣedha-varga*).
The section from the end of the "Refutation of the Self" (Pudgalaviniścaya) onwards is well-expounded as the "Correct Teaching" (Śāstramūla).
That which follows this is called the "Circulation Section" (Pravartanabhāga).
This treatise as a whole provides a comprehensive explanation of the selflessness of all phenomena within the sūtras; therefore,
the "Chapter on Refuting the Self" is also included within the main body of the work.
Although it appears at the end of the section on Concentration (Samādhi),
because its expressions of lamentation and exhortations to study precede the Main Body (Śāstra), it is also termed the "Main Body."
The second interpretation states:
The introductory section is the same as before.
Regarding the passage beginning with "What dharma is called... and so forth:
The section on Concentration (Samādhi) is titled the "Main Body" (Śarīra).
From the end of the section on Concentration down to the preceding analysis [of the preceding sections].
This is collectively termed the "Circulation" (Pravartana) section.
The reason why the "Refutation of the Self" (Pudgala-nairātmya) chapter is also called the Circulation section is that it initiates its inquiry from within the Circulation section;
furthermore, it is taught as a supplement situated after the Circulation section.
It is also called "Circulation. The third interpretation states:
This treatise explains that all dharmas are without self (*anātman*) according to the sūtras;
the first eight chapters clarify that all dharmas possess substantial existence (*svabhāva*).
Excluding the adherence to the view of diminution,
there are three parts:
the introductory section and the main body are the same as those of the second master.
From the section beginning with "Previously,

before making distinctions" down to the end of the Chapter on Concentration (Samādhi) is called the Section on Circulation (Pravartana-bhāga). The final chapter, which clarifies non-self (*anātman*) to eliminate the attachment to superimposition (*samāropa*),
also consists of three parts.
Regarding the first two lines:
if one bypasses these and relies on something else, would there not still be an explanation?
This is called the "Introductory Section" (nidāna).

The section beginning with "The principle is fixedly non-existent" is designated as the *mūla* (the main body), and the section beginning with "Having well explained this" is designated as the *pariṇāmanā* (the dissemination).
These two meanings within the sūtra are thus explained;
for this reason, each [text] separately possesses three distinct parts. It follows that in all treatises (*śāstra*), the *mūla* is invariably present.

The introductory section (*nidāna*) and the concluding section (*parīndanā*) are not fixed as to their presence or absence. There are cases where there is an introductory section but no concluding section, such as in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
There are also cases where there is a concluding section but no introductory section.
As in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
the two parts may both exist,
as stated in this treatise, or both parts may be non-existent.
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, because the intentions of the various authors differ, within the introductory section (*nidāna*), there are two parts:
first, the explicit exposition of the introduction;
second, the detailed explanation according to specific inquiries.
This first verse correctly elucidates the introductory section (*nidāna*).
Within it, the first three lines clarify the sequence of homage and veneration.
The fourth sentence clarifies the introductory section on the occasion for the composition. "Taking refuge and paying homage" refers to taking refuge in and paying homage to the World-Honored One;
"occasioning" refers to occasioning the main body of the treatise.
Therefore, one first takes refuge and pays homage.
The subsequent section clarifies the motivation for undertaking this treatise. Question:
For what reason does the treatise begin with verses of praise and homage?
Explanation: [As follows:]
Fearing that demonic obstacles might arise and prevent the treatise from being completed,
[the author] praises the virtues [of the Buddha], pays homage, and requests his protective assistance;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
By means of words of praise and veneration, one eliminates all evil obstructions and manifests auspicious omens; furthermore,
it is explained that this is for the purpose of knowing that the World-Honored One possesses supreme merit.
One gives rise to faith and reverence toward the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma. Furthermore,
it is explained that one is like a filial son who reports all his actions to his parents.
The author of the treatise is likewise.
Now, wishing to compose this treatise, he first addresses the World-Honored One.
Generally speaking, regarding the various treatises, there is no fixed rule as to whether they begin with an expression of reverence or an exposition of the subject matter.
There are cases where there is homage and reverence but no formal undertaking,
as in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*; and there are cases where there is an undertaking but no homage and reverence,
as in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
In some cases, both introductory sections are present, as in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*; in other cases, both introductory sections are absent, as in the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
This is because each treatise follows the distinct intention of its author. Regarding the section on the homage:
The first two phrases clarify the three virtues of the Buddha;
the third phrase points to these virtues for the purpose of taking refuge and paying homage.
Regarding the preceding two phrases:
The initial characters clarify the person perfected through virtue;
"all" and those that follow [clarify the perfection of merit].
This clarifies the virtues accomplished by the person.
Since one distinguishes virtues based on the person,
the person is mentioned first.
Regarding the sequence of the virtues:
first, the use of the plural particle "various" (*nānā*) indicates the absence of factionalism;
one summons others by means of their virtues.
I take refuge in and pay homage to whoever possesses the three qualities.
Since the various non-Buddhists each claim their own teacher to be omniscient,
if I were to pay homage exclusively to Śākyamuni alone, [it would be partial].
Fearing that they might give rise to slander,
he set forth these words to silence their dissenting arguments; or perhaps, fearing that the Buddha’s transformative influence might reach sentient beings of shallow faculties,
he provisionally acted as their teacher to lead them toward the True Dharma.
Therefore, these various terms have been set aside.
These characters originated with the masters Mātṛceṭa and Āryadeva from the Western Regions.
All those who wish to offer their reverent homage set aside all other words;
the Master of the Treatise considers this to be consistent with reason.
Therefore, it is also said that "among the virtues accomplished by a person," the first six characters clarify the virtue of self-benefit,
while the subsequent phrase clarifies the virtue of benefiting others.
The reason why self-benefit is clarified first and benefiting others is clarified afterward is that if one does not benefit oneself, how can one benefit others?
As the Sūtra says: "A Bodhisattva acts for the sake of benefiting others."
Regarding the statement "the extinction of all kinds of darkness" as spoken from the perspective of intention (*āśaya*),
this clarifies the quality of self-benefit.
Darkness is of two kinds.
First, defiled ignorance;
second, non-defiled ignorance.
Cessation also has two types.
First is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

second is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). One attains cessation not through deliberation when all types of darkness are extinguished and non-afflicted ignorance is severed.
This reveals the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*): all darkness is extinguished, defiled ignorance is severed, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained.

This reveals the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). The two terms "darkness" (*tamas*) and "extinguished" (*nirodha*) apply to both [qualities]. Non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) [is also included].
It is called "all" because its types are numerous;
it is called "various" because the types of defiled ignorance are not numerous. Alternatively, "all" and "various" are synonyms for "eye."
Alternatively, although "all" (sarva) and "various" (pṛthak) are synonyms for "eye," here "all" is used in its broad sense, while "various" is used in its narrow sense.
As for why the defiled [factors] are not called "types" (prakāra): [it is because they do not possess distinct categories].
"Kind" (jāti) refers to a category.
The categories of non-afflicted ignorance are infinite;
therefore, it is called "kind. The categories of afflicted ignorance are not numerous.
Therefore, it does not mention "lineage" (*gotra*). Alternatively, it should have mentioned lineage;
it was either omitted for brevity, or intended to be implied, or because this term "lineage" applies to both locations, namely, within the virtues of self-benefit.
As for why the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is explained first and the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) afterwards:
because the quality of wisdom belongs exclusively to the Buddha, it is taught first;
whereas the quality of abandonment is also common to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is therefore explained later. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
The merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and for this reason it is explained first;
the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and for this reason it is clarified later.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the cause, which is wisdom, is explained first, and the result, which is abandonment, is clarified later. [This refers to] "pulling sentient beings out from the mire of birth-and-death."
This clarifies the virtue of benefiting others;
that is, it refers to pulling sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death.
This reveals the virtue of gratitude. They are called "sentient beings" (sattva) because they undergo manifold births and deaths.
Now, birth is inevitably followed by death;
yet, because birth can encompass death,
we speak of "sentient beings" (sattva).
Death does not necessarily entail rebirth, as in the case of entering nirvana;
for this reason, it is not said that "the multitude dies. Alternatively, by mentioning the beginning, the end is implied.
Even if there were other texts stating that "the multitude dies," [the same principle would apply].

By mentioning the latter, the former is revealed: because birth and death are boundless, profound, vast, and difficult to escape, they are likened to mud. "I pay homage to such a Teacher of Reality" indicates the virtues to which one pays homage.
These words refer to the three aforementioned virtues. Question: For what reason?
The Long Discourse states:
"The words of the Teacher of Reality manifest the virtue of benefiting others."
The commentary explains: "By speaking only of benefiting others, one's own benefit is revealed;
for whoever benefits others necessarily benefits themselves. Furthermore, it is explained:
"I pay homage to these three qualities."
Homage to the Teacher who acts in accordance with reality.
Thus, this refers collectively to the three qualities.
The Master [Vasubandhu] spoke thus to specifically manifest the virtue of benefiting others. Question:
For what reason does this treatise pay homage only to the three virtues and not to the Three Jewels?
The commentary states:

The meanings of the "three virtues" (triguṇa) and the "Three Jewels" (triratna) differ, as they are explained according to the specific intentions of the authors of the various treatises. This is a general clarification regarding these treatises.
The three virtues and the Three Jewels are not fixed as to their presence or absence;
sometimes the three virtues are mentioned without reference to the Three Jewels.
According to such treatises, some explain the Three Jewels (triratna) without mentioning the three virtues (triguṇa), as in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*; others explain both types together;
there must likewise be textual evidence for this.
However, this has not yet been verified; perhaps both [the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Jñānaprasthāna*] do not state it.
As explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, this treatise also pays homage to the Jewel of the Buddha.
Furthermore, it is explained that because this treatise also pays homage to the Dharma Jewel—
the fruit-dharma of nirvāṇa— it simultaneously manifests the Buddha within the context of the virtue of wisdom.
Because it refers specifically to the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), the term "Saṃgha" is not explicitly mentioned;
this is either an abbreviation or a deliberate omission. Alternatively, the four stages of approach and the four fruits (*catur-śrāmaṇya-phala*) are designated as the Saṃgha.
This is the view of the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
One asaṃkhyeya kalpa was nearly completed;
because his wisdom surpassed theirs,
they did not pay him homage.
Question: For what reason does the Master of the Treatise also pay homage to the Saṃgha within his *Abhidharmasamuccaya*?
Explanation:
"Sangha" refers to a multitude.
In the Mahāyāna, there may be many bodhisattvas who simultaneously enter the state of sainthood.
Famous monks pay homage;
in this school, there is only one Bodhisattva.
One who has attained entry into the thirty-four moments of mind is not yet called a Saṃgha;
therefore, one does not take refuge in or pay homage to them. Another interpretation states:
This treatise also pays homage to the Jewel of the Saṅgha, as it simultaneously reveals the Saṅgha among those who possess the quality of gratitude.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "By the hand of the teaching of the True Dharma, they are pulled out and delivered."
"To rescue sentient beings and cause them to emerge from the three realms" thus reveals the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha also provides this interpretation; as for the statement in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, "I shall now speak," [it refers to this].
This clarifies the introductory section on the undertaking.

Having finished paying homage to the World-Honored One,
he granted permission for the commencement of the discourse, saying, "I shall now speak.
Desiring next to compose the treatise, he first provides this prologue.
The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'proceeding to prostrate with reverence,' this first section within the prose exposition provides a general indication of the meaning of the verses."
Second, the detailed explanation of the verse.
This is the general heading:
the Master now intends to compose the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra.
Although he summoned others by means of his virtue, his original intent was to manifest Śākyamuni as his own teacher;
for the essence of that virtue is so venerable and sublime that it transcends all those of the two vehicles and the assembly of bodhisattvas.

various non-Buddhists and others refer to themselves as the noble assembly. As for what is indicated by the plural "various": it refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The following provides a specific explanation.

the word "all," though general in scope, still specifically denotes the World-Honored One.
Because this can destroy darkness, it is called "the extinguisher of obscurity" (*tamo-nirghāta*).
This serves as a response to an anticipated objection.
The intent of the objection is as follows:
The term "all" is a general designation;
how, then, does it signify the Buddha?
Therefore, it is now explained comprehensively.
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses wisdom capable of destroying two kinds of darkness;
therefore, he is called the World-Honored One.
Both forms of darkness are extinguished.
Because the two types of darkness have been extinguished by the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, the plural pronoun "all" (sarva), although used generally, still refers specifically to the World-Honored One. Furthermore,
it is explained that this passage specifically reveals the person capable of destroying darkness.
Because this power of the Buddha can forever destroy all darkness, he is called the World-Honored One who extinguishes the obscure.
Regarding the phrase "all kinds" up to "all categories of darkness," it refers to the extinction of the darkness concerning all objects.
It severs defiled ignorance.
All objects are precisely the four truths and the path of cultivation.
Because one is deluded regarding these objects, it is termed "darkness" (moha).
This explains the extinction of all obscurations;
thus, the *Nyāya* states:
"Because the obscurations regarding all objects are also eternally extinguished."
The perfection of the virtue of abandonment refers to the cessation of all categories of darkness and the abandonment of non-afflicted ignorance.
"All categories" means all the various classes of phenomena (*dharma*).
Because one is deluded regarding this category, it is called "darkness" (*tamas*).

Question: Why does the verse first mention "all," while the long prose explains it later?
The commentary states:

Seeking [the truth] through its nature and characteristics, one speaks as the occasion demands;
how can there be fixed priority or sequence? Question: What constitutes the essence of the virtue of wisdom and the virtue of abandonment?
The commentary explains:
The quality of wisdom (jñāna-guṇa) takes the wisdom within the Buddha’s body as its essence;
if one includes the five aggregates that accompany it, they also constitute its essence. The quality of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa) takes analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) as its essence.

First, the abandonment of all afflictions;
second, the abandonment of all obstacles to meditative concentration;
third, ultimate abandonment.

This applies to the attainment of both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation.
This distinguishes [the sharp-facultied] from those of dull faculties.

The commentary states:
The virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa) takes analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) as its essence;
however, if one considers its broader application, it also encompasses non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, it is explained that the virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa) has only analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) as its essence;
however, because of the presence of hindrances to meditative concentration (samādhi-āvaraṇa) and so forth, this analytical cessation is not manifest.
If the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) and so forth were not [subject to] analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), they would simply be manifest;
because it is capable of manifesting their abandonment, it is called the "perfection of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-saṃpad*).
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that all four types of abandonment mentioned in that text are analytical cessations.
If the afflictions are abandoned, it is abandonment by way of their intrinsic nature;

if the bonds of the objects of perception are abandoned, it is abandonment by way of the bonds of the objects. If the hindrances to meditative concentration are abandoned, along with their latencies, this is abandonment by way of the bonds of the objects.
If it is ultimately severed— severed by its own nature and severed from its objects and fetters—
and because various forms of ignorance have arrived, it is called "darkness.
This explains the meaning of "darkness" (*tamas*).
Defiled and non-defiled ignorance are not one;
they are termed "various ignorances."

that which can obstruct true vision is afflicted ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*). Furthermore, another interpretation states:
"that which can obscure the true meaning" refers to obscuring external objects.
That which can obstruct true vision refers to the obstruction of the internal mind.
Both "to cover" and "to obstruct" carry the sense of obscurity, applying to both types of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Question: What constitutes the essential nature of defiled ignorance?
The commentary explains:
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is taken as the essence; therefore, other afflictions (*kleśa*) are not mentioned, because ignorance universally associates with all delusions.
If it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) also reveals other afflictions, one asks:
what is the meaning of "non-afflicted nescience" (*akliṣṭājñāna*)?
The explanation says:
To explain this meaning,
it will be briefly analyzed by way of three sections:
first, the determination of its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, the explanation of the name;
third, the analysis by way of various categories.
Within the section on establishing the essential nature, the first part sets forth divergent views.
Second, refuting errors;
third, stating the correct meaning. Regarding the statement "narrating divergent views," this refers to the assertions of persons and treatises.
There are eleven masters in total. The first master says:
"Non-defiled ignorance exists because one has not yet attained Buddhahood."
The first [master] says its essence consists of dull, maturation-born, and neutral minds and mental factors.
The second master says it is non-defiled ignorance,
which persists until one has attained Buddhahood.
The dull [ignorance] has the four types of neutral mind and mental factors as its essence. Regarding this, the third [master], the Western teacher Guṇaprabha, states:
"Non-afflicted ignorance exists until one attains Buddhahood."
The dull, intrinsically indeterminate mind has mental factors as its substance, yet it is not subsumed under the four types of indeterminate states;
it pervades the three realms and is always established in both the past and the future. Thus says the fourth master.
Non-defiled ignorance has,
until the attainment of Buddhahood,
the dull commonality of sentient beings as its essence.
The wisdom and other faculties arising based on this homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) perceive objects without clarity;
the fifth master calls this "non-afflicted ignorance" (akliṣṭājñāna).
Because its essence consists in the lack of mastery, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), in its exposition of the essence of the obstacles to liberation,
states: "Other masters say that this obstacle to liberation..."
It has as its essence the lack of mastery over the various meditative concentrations.
The sixth master says that non-defiled ignorance has non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as its essence.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 70,
states: "Other masters say that this is the obstacle to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*)."
The seventh teacher says that non-afflicted ignorance (akliṣṭājñāna) has the failure to diligently seek [the truths] and so forth as its essential nature.
It does not take the various meditative absorptions (samādhi) as its essence.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 70, states: "Other masters say:
because one does not diligently seek it during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*)."
Because they have not heard [the teaching] and have not practiced it repeatedly,
liberation does not arise.
This is precisely what is called the essence of the obstacle to liberation. The eighth master says:
"Non-defiled ignorance has wisdom as its non-active essence."
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), volume 28, in explaining the distinction between the two types of ignorance (*ajñāna*), states:
"Some say that if something can obstruct wisdom, it is defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*); non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is merely the absence of wisdom. The commentary explains:
The essence of this ignorance is able to obstruct the clarity of wisdom;
the essence that acts as the obstruction is defiled non-cognition (*kliṣṭājñāna*).
Where there is no wisdom, it is said to be non-defiled. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
This is the position of the Sautrāntika masters. The ninth master states:
non-afflicted ignorance has the collective latencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind and mental factors as its essence.
Therefore, the *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), chapter twenty-eight, states:
"The mind and its objects are collectively termed 'habitual tendencies' (*vāsanā*). The commentary explains:
although the *Nyāyabindu* does not provide a separate analysis [of this], [the meaning is as follows].
According to the ancient masters who refute this, there is such a teaching:
the latencies (*vāsanā*) belonging to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are collectively termed "ignorance" (*ajñāna*).
Regarding whether these latencies of ignorance are broad or narrow, the tenth master says:
Non-defiled ignorance is precisely what is called habitual tendency (*vāsanā*);
it possesses a distinct substantial nature within the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 28, states:
"An ancient master spoke of the characteristics of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), saying:
'There is a distinct mental factor (*caitta*) that is non-defiled.'"
The defiled and undefiled dharmas,
induced by repeated practice,
do not constitute the continuum of an omniscient one.
Manifest activity causes the mind and mental factors to function without mastery;
this is called habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
The commentary states:
"The ancient masters" refers to the ancient masters of the Sarvāstivāda school.
This is the explanation of the ancient masters:
among the mental factors (caitta), there is a distinct entity called "habitual tendency" (vāsanā).
This is non-cognition regarding the untainted.
The essence of the non-cognition regarding habitual tendencies has neither breadth nor narrowness.
It is like how non-cognition regarding the tainted is distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is induced by the repeated practice of all defiled and undefiled phenomena;
until the attainment of Buddhahood,
it arises in constant succession within every state of mind.
The mind that arises simultaneously with it does not function with autonomy;
although it is universally associated with all three natures (trividha-svabhāva), it remains subject to their influence.
However, its essence is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). The eleventh master says:
"Non-defiled ignorance has *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) as its essence."
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
The Venerable Śrīlāta has made this assertion:
"There exists a non-defiled dharma called 'habitual tendency' (*vāsanā*)."
Just as the maturation (vipāka) is summoned by unwholesome causes,
so too did the Blessed One, while formerly in the state of a bodhisattva,
cultivate all the preparatory practices (prayoga) throughout three incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa).
Although afflictions still exist,
one is able to gradually eliminate the non-afflicted habitual tendencies induced by those afflictions,
while causing the habitual tendencies of pure dharmas to gradually increase.
When he attains the permanent eradication of all outflows (*āsrava*),
some of his prior habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are extinguished while others are not,
because he has cultivated the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) over a long period of time.

nevertheless, the Buddha still possesses the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) of pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), for it is said that these residual impressions may be either extinguished or not extinguished. The commentary explains:

for those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the state of no-more-learning,

one should be called a Buddha.

If [the Buddha-nature] were not yet established at the time of its subsequent arising, it could not be called "Buddha";
yet if it has not yet arisen and is not yet established, it ought to be called "Buddha.
If you say that it is not called "Buddha" because of the presence of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), [then this is incorrect].
This implies that [the Buddha] would not be called a Buddha by virtue of those [factors].
How, then, would this concern the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors?
Therefore, it is said to be illogical. To refute the second master, he says:
If non-defiled ignorance were to have the four types of neutral minds as its essence,
then the unobscured-neutral mind would not be present in the desire and form realms.
In the case of those who have committed transgressions against the precepts, those who have not yet attained the formless realm, and those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa),
the mind born of maturation (vipākaja-citta) does not manifest before them.
It is not the case that [the Buddha] has not yet attained perfection;
he should therefore be called a Buddha.
Thus, [your position] is also irrational.
If it is argued that one is not called a Buddha because [the afflictions] necessarily arise and because there are residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā), [then this is incorrect].
This is refuted by the same arguments as previously cited;
therefore, it is also illogical. Refuting the third master, he says:
"If non-afflicted ignorance has a nature that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)—such as the mind and so forth—as its essence..."
Regarding the claim that [the past and future] are always established throughout the three realms,
although there is no fault of non-establishment,
it nevertheless contradicts the fourteen points of the *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*.
In that treatise, it is explained that among the twelve types of mind,
when one is born into the formless realm, the mind produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) does not manifest,
and one does not possess the unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*).
Since this contradicts that teaching, it is likewise unreasonable. Refuting the fourth master, he says:
"If it were non-cognition of the undefiled..."
As for the claim that its essence consists of the "homogeneous group" (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
this might perhaps be asserted as a distinct interpretation; however,
upon examining all the treatises, no such passage exists at all.
Therefore, this too is unreasonable. Refuting the fifth teacher, it says:
If one takes lack of sovereignty (*asvatantrya*) as the essence of the obstacle, the *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Logic), Chapter 7, refutes this, stating:
There must necessarily be some slight force of dharma acting as an obstacle,
causing him to lack mastery over meditative concentration; were it not so,
[he would have attained it].
What is the reason that he does not attain mastery over the various meditative concentrations? The explanation states:
there must certainly be some minor non-defiled ignorance regarding these dharmas. This refutes the sixth teacher.
If one takes non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as the essence of an obstruction,
the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise Following Reasoning), fascicle 70, refutes this, saying:
"As for 'non-acquisition,' it is definitely..."
It must have a cause.
It cannot be said that the cause is unobtainable,
for a self-essence ought not to depend upon itself.
Alternatively, the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) should also be said to have the non-attainment of the fruit of arhatship as its nature;
yet, that is not the case.
Why is this so? Refuting the seventh teacher, it says:
"If one takes 'not seeking diligently' and so forth as the essence of the obstacle, the *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Logic), chapter seven, refutes this, saying:"
The fruit of arhatship likewise cannot arise in its essential nature due to such factors as not seeking it with diligent application of effort.
How could it be that there is no distinct substance for the afflictive hindrance? Refuting the eighth master, [the text] says:
"If non-afflicted ignorance has wisdom as its unconditioned substance..."
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 28, states:
An ancient master refuted this, saying:
"It is not merely that wisdom is absent."
Regarding the impossibility of that which lacks capacity to serve as a cause: the refutation of the ninth teacher states,
"If non-defiled ignorance were to take the mind and mental factors collectively termed 'habitual tendencies' (vāsanā) as its essential nature," [it would be untenable].
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 28,
records that ancient masters critiqued this, saying: "One should not say that such types of mind and mental factors are collectively termed 'habitual tendencies' (*vāsanā*)."
Because non-defiled ignorance has already been explained previously;
that is to say, this ignorance takes the mind abiding in its own nature (*prakṛtisthacitta*) and so forth as its essence.
There would be a distinction [between Buddhas and others].
If the essence consists of the mind abiding in its own nature and so forth,
then even a Buddha would possess non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
If there were distinctions,
that which could differentiate them would be devoid of cognition.
It is not the case that there is no differentiation.
For when we observe the various categories of mind and mental factors— such as the wholesome and so forth—
there must necessarily be distinct dharmas that act as the differentiators.
It is not the case that all [factors] are present;
for instance, within the category of wholesome factors, faith and so forth must necessarily exist,
whereas within the category of unwholesome factors, there may or may not be shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth.
Within the category of defilements, there are factors such as heedlessness (*pramāda*). In such cases,
among the mind and mental factors, there must necessarily be distinct dharmas that function as the differentiators.
Thus we know that within this there is also a distinct factor capable of acting as a differentiator; this refers to non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
According to the commentary on this refutation, it is known that there is a "school of total calculation" (*sarvaga-samudāya-vāda*). The tenth ancient master’s refutation states: [text follows].
If nescience (*ajñāna*) were not defiled,
and if it were a distinct entity among the mental factors (*caitta*),
the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Conformance to Reasoning), fascicle 28, states:
The Master of Righteousness (Zhengyijia) says:
"Now, upon careful examination,
his statement contains excessive errors."
Ordinary worldlings, in their various minds and mental factors,
do not all correctly awaken to the characteristics of taste, potency, and maturation as they truly are.
However, since no other minds or mental factors are observed to arise,
and since those minds and mental factors arise as distinct entities in each and every moment,

it would follow that in every moment there must arise separate and distinct non-cognitive phenomena. If you argue that there are differing characteristics that cause this distinction in non-cognition, [the same fault remains].
This is precisely the category of mind that possesses specific distinctions (*viśeṣa-viśeṣa-citta*).
Why, then, must non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) be reckoned separately? The explanation says:
if this dharma were to function constantly during the stage of non-comprehension (*ajñāna-avasthā*), [it would be redundant].
Since all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas lack such understanding,
they should all equally possess ignorance.
In reality, however, one does not perceive it arising as a distinct category of mind;
rather, it is produced only by various mental factors such as the wholesome.
If it is argued that this factor is not incompatible with anything and is always associated in every moment of thought:
There must be differentiation because there is differentiation among the associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
It is by virtue of that differentiation that the associated factors arise as distinct entities.
If it is argued that "differentiation" refers to having different characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), [then...]
That very characteristic of difference causes each category of mind to be individually ignorant.
Why trouble yourself with a separate doctrine? The *Commentary on the Eleven Gates* (*Ekādaśamukha-śāstra*) states:
"If non-cognizance that is not defiled takes habitual tendencies as its essence..."
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 28, refutes this,
saying: "While the reasoning thus stated may indeed be so,
it is unable to manifest its essential nature."
What is the nature of the undefiled habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*)?

the term "habitual tendencies" is used in a general sense.

thus, in the end, it results in erroneous discourse. Third, regarding the exposition of the correct meaning:
non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
Because, until one has attained Buddhahood,
all contaminated, non-defiled, and inferior wisdom constitutes its essence.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 28, states:
Therefore, regarding taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and so forth,
there is no wisdom that seeks understanding with diligence.
Coexisting with phenomena of a different characteristic,
it acts as a cause that induces and gives rise to a cognition of the same class.
This wisdom does not diligently seek understanding; furthermore,
it serves as the cause that induces the production of a wisdom that does not diligently seek understanding.
Thus, through this continuous succession from beginningless time,
cause and effect have followed one another until they have been practiced into the very nature of beings.
Therefore...
Regarding those objects such as tastes, the repeated practice of a cognition that lacks the capacity for comprehension induces an inferior wisdom;
this is termed non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). This very [ignorance], together with the co-emergent mind and mental factors, is collectively designated as "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
