Its essence is the lack of mastery over meditative absorption. Some say that various absorptions themselves do not constitute its essence;
although the *Vibhāṣā* contains no formal adjudication on this point, [this is the view].
According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, the first master’s position is taken as correct.
Thus, in the seventy-fifth chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra*, regarding the essential nature of the obstacle to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*), there are four masters in total. The first master says:
There is an inferior, ignorant, and non-obscured neutral nature that can obstruct liberation;

this constitutes the essence of the obstacle to liberation. A second master holds that its essence is lack of mastery (*asvatantrya*). A third master holds that its essence is non-attainment (*aprāpti*). A fourth master holds that its essence is a lack of diligent seeking and so forth. Furthermore, it is said:
Because it was taught first as being consistent with reason.
Those three masters’ explanations are exactly as previously stated;
by means of this textual evidence, it is known.
Its essence consists of non-defiled ignorance and inferior wisdom.
Furthermore, Master Yuanyu, in his commentary on the passage beginning with "Or those sentient beings who have already [attained] the *Nyāyānusāra*," states:
"By means of various non-defiled minds..."
Furthermore, within the continuum of the body,
there are various afflictions that have perfumed it into latent dispositions;
this refers to those in whom ignorance is predominant.
Even when wholesome states of mind manifest,
they are for the most part obscure and conform to ignorance;
other cases are likewise.
Based on these habitual tendencies,
this is termed "ignorance.
What is its essential nature?
Until one attains Buddhahood,
all contaminated wholesome and indeterminate dharmas [are included].
Because it accords with ignorance and opposes thorough knowledge,
all such states are termed "non-knowledge."
In this way, the category of the defiled (kliṣṭa) is also with outflows (sāsrava) and is subsumed under the defiled.
Therefore, this is not discussed here. Thus,
regarding the stage where what is to be abandoned by insight has already been eliminated—
namely, from the stage of a stream-enterer up to that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Both the defiled and non-defiled categories possess the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
This excludes only the untainted (*anāsrava*),
because the name "defiled" refers to the category of afflictive types.
That which is undefiled is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*) because it is formed by the habitual afflictions.
This [passage] generally refers to any undefiled yet outflowing (*sāsrava*) mind or body that accords with the afflictions, as it resembles the afflictions.
These are termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
They are non-afflicted ignorance and habitual-tendency ignorance.
There is neither expansion nor contraction;
the Buddha-body ultimately does not conform to afflictions,
for it has severed their habitual tendencies.
This is called the "purified continuum.
One is designated as "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) only when one no longer trains in wisdom.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names:
because its essence is not defiled, it is called "non-defiled" (akliṣṭa);
because it does not awaken to objects, it is termed "ignorance" (ajñāna).
Ignorance that is itself non-defiled is called "non-defiled ignorance" (*akliṣṭājñāna*);
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It is also termed "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyabindu* states:
"This non-afflicted ignorance is precisely what is called 'habitual tendency' (*vāsanā*)."
Regarding the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*):
"habit" (*xi*) refers to repeated practice;
"tendency" (*qi*) refers to a residual portion.
There are various afflictions (*kleśa*) and inferior cognitions (*hīnajñāna*), among which there are numerous portions of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Therefore,
they are called "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*),
because they are the residual traces (*vāsa*) of habituation (*vāsana*).
It is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
Alternatively, it is explained that the habitual tendency itself is named "tendency."
There is a portion of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) cultivated by various afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth;
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It is also called "the wisdom that does not diligently seek liberation" or "incapable wisdom."
It is sometimes called inferior knowledge (*hīnajñāna*), or inferior ignorance (*hīnājñāna*),
as stated in the *Nyāya*, or it is called inferior non-knowledge (*hīnājñāna*).
It is also called "false wisdom" (*mithyājñāna*), as stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. These various names differ in terminology but are identical in essence;
this can be understood through reflection. Third, the analysis by way of categories:
First, the differentiation of defilement and purity;
second, the distinction between the breadth and narrowness of cultivation and clarity;
third, the analysis according to the three natures.
Fourth, the explanation of the stages of abandonment (*prahāṇāvasthā*).
Regarding the first point, the differentiation according to defilement (*saṃkleśa*),
the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* provides three interpretations in total.
The first interpretation states:
"Now, upon careful examination,
the characteristics of these two kinds of ignorance are distinct."
That is to say, it is by virtue of this that the distinction between the ignorant and the wise is established;
such is called the characteristic of defiled ignorance.
If, by virtue of this...
"In some objects, wisdom does not reach the level of the foolish; this is the second characteristic. The commentary states:
"Foolish" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
"wisdom" refers to noble ones (*ārya*).
The distinction between these two arises from defiled ignorance:
those who have severed it are called noble ones (ārya), while those who have not severed it are called ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).
If, due to this non-afflicted ignorance, there is a distinction between light and heavy [degrees of obscuration],
then among various objects,
there may be an Arhat who does not recognize red salt.
However, there are ordinary beings who are well-versed in the Three Piṭakas;
this is called ignorance regarding the inability [to discern] objects and knowledge. A second interpretation states:
furthermore, if [the afflictions] have already been severed...
The Buddhas and those of the Two Vehicles are without distinction;
this is the first characteristic.
If it has been severed, then...
The Buddha and those of the two vehicles differ in that [the former] has practice while [the latter] lack it;
this is the second characteristic of understanding,
which refers to defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*).
The three vehicles are identical in their abandonment [of defilements] and in their non-manifestation;
this is called "no distinction.
Alternatively, they are identical in their realization of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this is called "no distinction."
Although non-defiled ignorance is likewise severed by all three vehicles regarding its objective fetters,
it manifests in the two vehicles but does not manifest in the Buddha.
The third explanation states:
Furthermore, if one is deluded regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena,
this is called the first characteristic of defiled ignorance.
If one cannot, with regard to all phenomena, realize as they truly are their characteristics such as taste, potency, maturation, quality, number, measure, location, time, similarity, and difference.
This is called non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). The commentary explains:
if one is deluded regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of various phenomena, this is afflicted ignorance;
however, if one is [deluded] regarding the subtle distinctions among various dharmas...

The "taste" (*rasa*) of all phenomena refers to their flavor, such as the taste of suffering and so forth. The "force" (*vega*) of all phenomena refers to their power to project subsequent self-results.

The "maturation" (*pāka*) of all phenomena refers to the power of their actual arising—whether it be detrimental or beneficial—to bring about their own results; this is termed "maturation" (*pāka*), "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), or "attainment" (*niṣpatti*). The "qualities" (*guṇa*) of all phenomena refer to their functional attributes, such as the number one, two, etc., quantity such as large or small, spatial location such as near or far, temporal duration such as recent or distant, similarity among similar phenomena, and differentiation among distinct phenomena. These are their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The inability to realize [things] as they truly are is non-afflicted ignorance.
Regarding the second pair, "familiarity" and "clarity," there is a distinction between breadth and narrowness.
Nescience is narrow while habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are broad.
Non-defiled nescience is necessarily an habitual tendency; however, there are habitual tendencies that are not nescience, namely the co-emergent mind and mental factors associated with nescience.
Regarding the third [point], the differentiation of the three natures of all habitual tendencies (vāsanā) within the continuum of the body:
non-afflicted ignorance (akliṣṭājñāna) is categorized as both wholesome and unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Since it is described as "non-afflicted," [it is not unwholesome].
It is clear that it is neither unwholesome nor obscured-neutral.
If it were wholesome,
it would be constantly accomplished by those in the formless realm and by those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Could one not then be called a Buddha?
If it were exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
then the formless (*ārūpya*) and non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) minds born of maturation (*vipākaja*) would never manifest.
Because it is not [merely] unaccomplished, it should be called "Buddha.
For this reason, it is also categorized as wholesome (*kuśala*). Question:
If it is wholesome, why does the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 9, state:
Question: What is this false wisdom?
Answer: It is the wisdom characterized by the aspect of non-obscured, neutral wrong conduct, which is to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
Just as one might perceive a person in a tree stump,
or perceive a tree stump in a person,
or perceive a path where there is no path.
One conceives the notion that the path is not the path.
Regarding such cases, the *Saptati-śāstra* (Treatise on the Seventy [Verses]) further states:
"There exists an inferior, ignorant, non-obscured, and indeterminate nature that is capable of obstructing liberation."
Regarding the nature of this obstacle to liberation,

it is further said that all the great masters of the treatises unanimously declare that the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is entirely for the purpose of eliminating the power of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and meditation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) which have been induced [by those obstacles].
Regarding the manifestation of non-obscured neutral ignorance, according to those two treatises,
it is simply referred to as "neutral.
The commentary explains:
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that because the cognition of the characteristics of wrong conduct is not true knowledge, it is termed "wrong";
therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* provides an explanation of the essential nature of the obstacles to liberation and the essential nature of the obstacles to the faculties.
Therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Now, since this generally reveals the essential nature of all non-defiled ignorance,
it is also categorized as "wholesome" (kuśala).
Alternatively, there are two types of ignorance:
first, that which is obscured by wholesome dharmas and thus weak in power;
second, that which is obscured by neutral dharmas and thus predominant in power.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, speaking according to what is predominant,
therefore state that it is "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
The statement that it also extends to the wholesome is based on the inferior [type of wholesome]. Furthermore, another interpretation holds:
since all treatises state that non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is clear that it does not extend to the wholesome.
Although there are times when it does not constitute an unobscured-neutral mind or mental factors— because [the latter] necessarily arise and because there is habitual tendency (vāsanā)—
it is not called "Buddha."
Although there are two interpretations, the former is superior in meaning.
If one were to challenge the latter position, it should be explained by analogy with the former. Fourth, regarding the clarification of the stages of abandonment:
this refers to non-defiled ignorance.
If a bodhisattva gradually abandons [defilements] according to their respective stages over three incalculable eons,
they only completely abandon all faults upon reaching the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Although those of the two vehicles and so forth do indeed partially abandon them, [they do not do so in this manner].
This is not a case of severing a fault.

One should understand that what is here called "severance" refers to the ultimate non-arising [of a phenomenon], which is termed "severance" because it attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This does not refer to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

If it were based on analytical cessation, then since the three vehicles would equally abandon it, there would be no distinction between them. Question: When a bodhisattva abandons non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*), [how is this distinguished from the others]?
One attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). At what stage is it attained?
The explanation says:

Only upon reaching the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) are they completely severed and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) attained. Question: Regarding the defiled ignorance abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it certainly does not function at the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
Therefore, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, the thirty-four moments of non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) will certainly not occur.
Why is it that non-analytical cessation is not attained at the very first stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)? The explanation is as follows:
The attainment of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is based solely on the deficiency of conditions;
that cessation is attained precisely when the superior conditions are absent.
This occurs at the time of the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi).
Because the superior conditions for undefiled ignorance are simply lacking,
one attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) at this stage,
as is the case with conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realizations (abhisamaya-antya-saṃvṛti-jñāna), and so forth.
Although its essential nature is ultimately non-arising and it does not emerge from meditative equipoise even during the preceding stages,
this occurs at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the three truths.
Because the superior conditions are lacking, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the three types of direct realization (*abhisamaya*) as follows:
"It means that at that time, one gives rise to mastery over attainment."
"Because of obstacles from other conditions, its essence does not manifest"—this concludes the treatise. The same principle applies to non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
As for afflicted ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*), it is abandoned at the stage of *adhimātra-kṣānti* (supreme patience).
Furthermore, because non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is also attained through the absence of superior conditions,
this does not constitute a valid analogy. According to the explanation of the Western masters,
it is even possible to emerge from meditative equipoise within thirty-four moments of thought.
This does not constitute a valid objection;
one should understand that this treatise designates non-arising based on evidence as "cessation," and speaks specifically of the future.
If one bases this on the fact that it is not yet established and thus designates it as "cessation," this also applies to the past; however,
it is only when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, arrives that it is called "extinction."

This explains the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*). It distinguishes [this] solely from the Two Vehicles. "Accomplishment" means attainment; "non-retrogression" means permanent counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).
There are two kinds of counteraction: first, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
Second is the thorough awakening to all objects as they truly are;
that is, to the four truths and the path of cultivation in all their aspects.
That is to say, there are two kinds of darkness (avidyā) of all types:
namely, the defiled and the non-defiled. Furthermore, there are two kinds of non-arising:
the first is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The second is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because its unconditioned nature is eternal, it is said not to arise;
this applies only to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Because one has attained the noble path as the ultimate antidote,
one realizes the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)— the state of non-arising— with respect to all objects of defiled ignorance concerning both principles and phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "cessation" (nirodha), because one attains the permanent antidote through realization in accordance with reality.
Regarding all types of non-afflicted darkness,
one realizes the state of non-arising through non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Therefore, it is called "cessation.
The phrase "śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas [attain it] up to,
but not in every respect" cites the inferior to highlight the superior.
Although the followers of the two vehicles are equal to the World-Honored One in having extinguished all darkness,
they are called "followers of the two vehicles" because they have only brought about the ultimate cessation of defiled ignorance.
Because they have not severed all types of non-afflicted ignorance,
they are not called Buddhas. Why is this so?
Question: How is it known that the two vehicles have not severed all types of darkness, given that they have not yet severed [darkness] even with respect to the Buddha-dharma?
Answer: The Buddha-dharma.
This refers to the dharmas such as the ten powers within the Buddha’s body. Furthermore,
it is explained that the dharmas known by the Buddha include those that are extremely distant, such as the most remote time.
This refers to the period beyond eighty thousand kalpas;
it refers to the locations in the most distant places, namely those beyond the trichiliocosm;
it refers to all categories of meaning, namely the infinite distinctions among the various categories of all phenomena (*dharma*).
Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet severed non-afflicted ignorance,
they do not know things that are extremely distant and so forth.
Because of this lack of knowledge,
it is shown that they are not capable of severing all types [of ignorance].
Nevertheless, various treatises state that the two vehicles are able to sever non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
This is the conclusion of the citation,
which summarizes what has already been praised regarding the Blessed One’s perfection of the virtue of benefiting others,
as explained through the severance of the bonds of conditions.
Regarding the reason why the extraction of sentient beings from [suffering] is compared to mud:
this refers to the specific explanation of the "mud of birth and death" (*saṃsāra-paṅka*) as set forth in the verse.
It is because of that birth and death [that they are so described].
These sentient beings are submerged in and immersed within it;
because it is difficult to emerge from, it is called a "place of submersion.
It is called a "place of immersion" because it is deep and because it is viscous. Because it is sticky, one finds it difficult to escape; therefore, it is likened to mud.
That is to say, karma and its maturation constitute the soil;
the afflictions constitute the water.
Their mutual intermingling is called the mire of saṃsāra.
"Birth-and-death is called 'mud.
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Alternatively, it is explained as "the mud of birth-and-death."
It takes all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as its essence,
because by means of them one undergoes many births and deaths; thus,
those in training (*śaikṣa*) gradually emerge from it.
If one is a person beyond training (aśaikṣa),
they are called "one who has emerged" because they will not undergo further existence after this present life. Another interpretation is as follows:
The mud of birth and death is called the "mud of birth and death.
Birth and death refers to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*),
while the mud refers to evil karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
If a person in training (śaikṣa) emerges from the mire of birth and death;
if a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) has completely emerged from the mire of birth and death and is further liberated—
this future birth and death is termed "mire."
If a person in training (śaikṣa) undergoes it again,
it is not yet called "emerging" (niḥsaraṇa);
one beyond training (aśaikṣa) does not undergo it.
It is called "emergence" (niḥsaraṇa).
Therefore, within the twelve links of dependent origination, those in the future are termed birth, old age, and death; it is regarding these that sentient beings are brought to rescue and emergence.
This explains the meaning of "deliverance.
Because sentient beings are submerged and drowning in the mire of birth and death,
there is no one capable of rescuing them.
The World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings;
with the hand of the true Dharma teachings of the three vehicles, he bestows them as appropriate and delivers them,
causing them to emerge [from suffering].
Therefore, the *Nyāyabhāṣya* states:
"By bestowing the teachings of the True Dharma, he pulls sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death;
thus, his beneficent virtue is perfected. Question: What constitutes the essence of this beneficent virtue?
The commentary states:
Its essence consists of great compassion;
alternatively, according to its accompanying factors, its essence consists of the five aggregates.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:

"Those who possess skillful wisdom and great compassion bestow appropriate words to rescue and deliver [beings] from [suffering]. In that treatise, skillful wisdom is precisely great compassion; alternatively, it may be understood thus.
The nature of this grace consists of skillful wisdom and great compassion.
Having thus praised the Buddha’s virtues, the subsequent expression of homage serves as a transitional link.
"Homage to him who is thus called the Teacher according to Reality.
"Kai" (稽) means "to reach";
"shou" (首) means "head."
Because one receives the Buddha’s humility with one’s own honor, one says "I pay homage.
It is called "thus" (*evam*) because it refers collectively to the three virtues. It is "according to reality" (*yathābhūtam*) because it instructs sentient beings without error.
Causing them to practice wholesome dharmas and admonishing sentient beings so that they do not commit evil is called being a teacher who acts according to principle.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 16) states:
"It is called 'instruction' (*avavāda*) because it precludes what is unbeneficial;
it is called 'teaching' (*anuśāsana*) because it provides what is beneficial."
As explained at length therein,
regarding the words of the Teacher of Reality concerning the attainment of the *pranidhijñāna* (wish-fulfilling supernatural power):
although the three qualities were previously set forth in full, [the following is stated].
Now, furthermore, he shows particular reverence for the benefit of others.
This verse should state: "I pay homage to such qualities of benefiting oneself and others; I pay homage to the Teacher who acts in accordance with reality.
This refers to the quality of benefiting others.
Because this virtue of benefiting others excels in its benefit to sentient beings, he pays homage once more;
for it is solely through the true teaching that sentient beings are rescued and led out of birth-and-death,
not by the power of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) or the like.
One does not escape birth and death through the granting of boons by devas and other deities,
nor through the manifestation of supernatural powers.
These three can only provide temporary relief;
they cannot ultimately cause one to transcend birth and death.
What is the purpose of paying homage to the Teacher who acts in accordance with reality?
Question on the Meaning of Reverent Homage. Response:
Because this treatise reaches the depths of the Abhidharma-piṭaka, it is called a *śāstra*.
[The author] provides an answer in verse:
It is called a "treatise" (śāstra) because it instructs disciples to practice virtue and abandon evil. What,
then, is this treatise?
Question: Regarding the term "Abhidharmakośa" (Treasury of Abhidharma), what is meant by "Abhidharma"?
Answer:
What is meant by "Abhidharma"?
Below this is the second section, which provides a detailed explanation according to specific questions.
Within this, first,
the essence of the Abhidharma is presented.
Second, the explanation of the name of the Piṭaka;
third, the clarification of the intent of the teaching and the person who taught it.
This constitutes the presentation of the essence of the Abhidharma.
The preceding verse raises the question.
The verse says, "up to those who are masters of wisdom. This is the verse that provides the answer.
Pure wisdom along with its attendants is called Abhidharma;
furthermore, all wisdoms and treatises that can attain this untainted pure wisdom are also called Abhidharma.
In Sanskrit, it is called *Abhidharma*.
This is translated as "gāthā" (verse).
The old rendering "jie" (gāthā) is a corruption.
The treatise says: "As for 'up to the Abhidharma'..."
Within the prose section, there are two parts:
first, the definition of its essence;
second, the explanation of its name.
The following section sets forth the essential nature [of wisdom].

It explains the first line of the verse: "Wisdom" refers to the discernment of the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths; "pure" means untainted (*anāsrava*), because it is free from the two types of bondage.
Therefore, it is called "pure wisdom" (*viśuddha-prajñā*). Question: Why is wisdom specifically mentioned among the factors such as association (*samprayoga*) and co-existence (*sahabhū*)? Answer:
It is because wisdom alone possesses all three types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
Investigation is termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); the object of deliberation is termed "condition" (*ālambana*);
and that which brings about accomplishment is termed "matter" (*vastu*).
Therefore, only "name" (*nāman*) is specifically designated.
Other minds and mental factors have both objects and entities as their conditions, but lack both seeing and clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Other co-existent dharmas have only entities as their objects of clear realization and lack seeing;

they possess both [types of] conditions. Therefore, their names are not specifically mentioned. Alternatively, because wisdom (*prajñā*) is powerful in abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), its name alone is specifically mentioned. Question: Why are "pure patience" (*śuddhakṣānti*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) not referred to as "seeing" (*darśana*)?
Regarding the statement "pure wisdom," the commentary explains:
there are instances of patience that are not wisdom, such as the eight patiences (*aṣṭakṣānti*).

Knowledge (*jñāna*) that is not [simply] vision (*darśana*), such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), subsumes all three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because the term "knowledge" is broad in scope, it is established as "pure wisdom" (*viśuddha-prajñā*) alone. Its retinue consists of those factors associated with wisdom, those co-existent with it, and its acquisitions (*prāpti*).
It is called "concomitant" (anuvartin). Question:
It is appropriate to call it "concomitant" because it is a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
However, acquisition (prāpti) is not a co-existent cause.
How is it that they are said to "follow along"?
The explanation says:
"Following along" means to accord with [the primary factor], not necessarily to act as its cause. It is asked: what dharma accompanies them?
The term "conformity" (*anuvartin*) refers to that which can be spoken of as occurring after the dharma;
since acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs prior to the dharma, how can it be said to "conform"?
The explanation is as follows:

The term "concomitance" (anuvartin) refers to the conformity of nature and characteristics; it does not necessarily require that they exist simultaneously before being termed "concomitant. Question: If this is indeed concomitance, why do various treatises, in their explanations of the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu), state: *“When one arises, the others arise; when one ceases, the others cease.”* This implies simultaneous arising and ceasing.
How can this be reconciled with the definition of concomitance as mere conformity?
It is not a concomitant (anuvartin).
Furthermore, in the third volume of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, regarding the explanation that "possession" (prāpti) is not co-existent with the supreme dharmas (agra-dharma), it states:
"Possession does not follow along with those dharmas."
According to those various treatises, it is understood that [this] is not a concomitant (anuvartin).
The explanation states:
there are two types of concomitance (*anuvartana*): first, that which is called "concomitance" by virtue of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Because the two are mutually conformable, they are called "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*).
There are also two types of "accompanying" (*anucara*): first, that which is called "accompanying" because it is a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*);
second, that which is called "accompanying" because it is mutually conformable. In various treatises, these are referred to by the terms "accompanying" and "concomitant."
According to the explanation based on conformity:

if various treatises state that "attainment" (*prāpti*) does not follow along or accompany [the dharma], this is based on its not being a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). Another interpretation states:
Based on that cited passage, it is established that [the factors] are not necessarily concomitants (*anuvartin*). Question:
Do the concomitants include wisdom (*prajñā*)? Answer: They do include wisdom.
Pure wisdom and its retinue are both termed "concomitants" (anuvartin),
because they follow one another in mutual succession. Thus,
it is stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81.
Regarding the essence of the immeasurable joy (*muditā*), it is said:
Joy has the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one includes its associated and concomitant factors, [it consists of all those mental states].
The desire realm has the four aggregates as its intrinsic nature;
the form realm has the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, in the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, among the three applications of mindfulness:
It is said that all applications of mindfulness regarding the analysis of mixed objects are comprised within wisdom (*prajñā*),
because among the three applications of mindfulness...
Only the application of mindfulness through the mixing of objects (*saṃmiśra-smṛtyupasthāna*) is able to sever the afflictions;
this will be fully cited and explained in the section on the applications of mindfulness.
Furthermore, it is explained that the "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*) does not include wisdom (*prajñā*).
They are called "concomitants" (anuvartin) because they proceed in accordance with wisdom;
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* bases this on their mutual concomitance,
while the *Nyāyānusāra* and *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vyākhyā* base it on their further intermingling.
Each [explanation] relies on a specific meaning and they do not contradict one another. Although there are two interpretations, the former interpretation is superior.
Thus, it is said in general that the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) are called Abhidharma.
This is the ultimate Abhidharma.
It is called "ultimate" (paramārtha) because it is untainted (anāsrava);
it is called "dharma" (artha) because it possesses meaning and function (arthakriyā).
"Victorious" (vibhūta) refers to "meaning" (artha);
thus, the ultimate meaning (paramārtha) is called Abhidharma.
This is an example of a *karmadhāraya* compound.
If it is said that from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) one reaches the Abhidharma,
this explains the latter part of the verse.
To say "conventional" refers to phenomena that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
That which obscures the true reality is called "worldly" (*loka*).
That which manifests as phenomenal characteristics in accordance with conventional sentiment is called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
Furthermore, it is explained that because contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are subject to destruction, they are so named.
Because it possesses an antidote,
it is called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). That which is worldly is called "conventional," and that which is conventional is called *abhidharma*.
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
That is to say, it refers to the various wisdoms and treatises of the Abhidharma that are capable of attaining this pure wisdom.
Regarding "wisdom," it refers to the various contaminated wisdoms that attain this pure wisdom of the Abhidharma.
Cultivated wisdom refers to the four roots of goodness, such as *uṣmagata* and so forth;
wisdom through reflection refers to the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The wisdom of hearing refers to the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-praśamana*).
The wisdom acquired at birth refers to the ability to receive and uphold the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
These four types of wisdom are explained here based solely on their single characteristic.

The gradual entry into the stage of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) according to its preceding and succeeding sequence does not yet fully accord with the ultimate principle. If one relies on the ultimate principle regarding common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
and the five stages of cessation (*pañca-nivaraṇa-pratipakṣa*),
all of these pertain to cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), contemplative wisdom (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), and scriptural wisdom (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).
This shall be analyzed below.
Regarding the four types of wisdom associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
they should be explained in their proper sequence according to the gradual order.
Now, because the noble path is categorized by its intimacy, remoteness, proximity, and distance, four [types of wisdom] are explained in reverse order. An ancient master stated:
"The wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) takes names as its object and is also capable of receiving, maintaining, reading, and reciting them. This interpretation is incorrect.
Because the *Vibhāṣā* is not entirely correct in its principles, the *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 42) states:
"The critique says: one should speak thus."

If one receives, maintains, recites, masters, and widely disseminates the Three Piṭakas and the twelvefold division of the teachings, this is the wisdom acquired through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhikā prajñā*). Question: Why is the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī prajñā*) not permitted [in this context]?
Regarding "receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting," the commentary explains:
if one hears correctly, it gives rise solely to innate wisdom (*upapattilābhajñāna*).
Because that which is established through hearing is called "wisdom derived from hearing," the nature of all four types of wisdom associated with outflows is wisdom itself.
If one distinguishes the accompanying factors (*anucara*), they all pertain to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Since both those acquired through reflection (*cintā-maya*) and those acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*) are capable of initiating karma,
and because they share the same nature, their essential characteristics are mutually concordant.
It is also called "concomitant" (anuvartin);
therefore, it pervades the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha). Question: How is it known that the two types of wisdom—those arising from hearing and reflection—are capable of initiating karma?
Answer: It is explained as follows:
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 42, states:
"Among the fruits of the various restraints (*saṃvara*),
there are those that arise from preparatory wholesome action (*prayoga-kuśala*)."
That which is produced:
there is that which is produced from a wholesome mind acquired at birth,
or that which arises from a wholesome mind resulting from application.
Regarding the ethical discipline (*saṃvara*), one first abandons it and subsequently severs the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of karma that results in marks (*lakṣaṇa-vipāka-karman*)?"
Is it bodily action?
Is it verbal action?
Or is it mental action?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature consists of the three types of action (*karman*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Question: Is the karma that results in the maturation of the marks (*lakṣaṇa-vipāka-karman*) that which is produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*), that which is produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*), or that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*)?"
Answer: It is accomplished solely through reflection;
it is neither through hearing nor through cultivation. Why is this so?
Because this karma is superior, it is not produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*);

because it is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is not produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*). Some say that this karma is produced by both hearing and reflection (*cintāmaya*), but is not produced by cultivation;
this is proven by the following passage.
Therefore, it is known that hearing and reflection can give rise to bodily and vocal [actions].
Question: If you say that hearing and reflection can give rise to bodily and vocal [actions], then since they can give rise to speech, [how is this so]?
One is then able to receive and uphold the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
Why, then, is it said that this is only "wisdom acquired at birth"?
The explanation is as follows:
Hearing and reflection can give rise to superior bodily and verbal actions;
however, those actions are not themselves superior, and thus they are produced solely through birth-attainment (*upapatti-pratilambhika*). Nevertheless, the ancient masters have said:
A preparatory wholesome mind cannot initiate bodily or vocal karma.
Citing *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* 47 as evidence, it asks:
"Do all wholesome minds of the form realm possess the concomitant morality (*anuvartaka-śīla*)?"
Answer: Not all possess it.
That is to say, in the first dhyāna there are six wholesome minds, but no concomitant morality (anuvartaka-śīla).
First, the excellent faculty of sight;
second, the excellent consciousness of hearing;
third, the excellent consciousness of touch.
Fourth, the wholesome mind at the time of death;
fifth, the wholesome mind that initiates informative action (*vijñapti*);
sixth, that which is associated with the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Regarding "wholesome mind," the ancient masters' intention was as follows:
Since the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Vibhāṣā*) states that the mind manifesting [action] is mentioned separately from the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*),
it is known that the wisdom of hearing cannot initiate karma.
An objection is raised:
"The end of life is what constitutes birth-attainment (*upapatti-lābhika*);
it is separately stated that birth-attainment alone is capable of initiating karma."
What prevents us from stating that, apart from the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), this wisdom can also initiate karma?
If it is argued that the mind at the moment of death is too weak to initiate karma,
then for that reason one must separately state that the mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*) initiates karma.
What prevents the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) from being that which initiates karma?
To say that the mind of wisdom derived from hearing can initiate karma is also subsumed within the mind that initiates karma;
therefore, this is not a definitive proof.
Moreover, since there are explicit scriptural texts [to the contrary],
one knows by this that the explanations of the ancient masters are unreasonable. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Regarding the statement that the four types of outflow-tainted wisdom (sāsrava-prajñā) are associated with and co-existent [with the path],

and are thus called "concomitants" (anucara) because they are co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu): the treatise explains that these are those which successively give rise to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā).
Because it is the most distant from the Noble Path when considered in terms of its perspective, it is explained after wisdom (*prajñā*).

Although these various types of wisdom differ in their relative proximity or distance from the Noble Path during the preceding stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), [they are all categorized here].
Because these are all the supreme provisions for the Noble Path, they may also be called *Abhidharma*.
As for the term "various treatises," this refers to the six *Pādas* and the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
It may be said that by mentioning the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), its branches are included; or it may be so.
The various treatises also include the *Mūla-śāstra*.
Regarding the "Six Feet" (*ṣaṭpāda*): Śāriputra composed the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*.
The *Dvādaśasāhasrikā* (12,000 verses);
the abridged version, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* (8,000 verses)—"Śāri" here refers to the śārika bird;
"zi" is the Chinese term for "son"; composed by Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this is the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*.
The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-maudgalyāyana* [Sūtra];
"Maudgalyāyana" is translated here as "Bean-gatherer's Descendant" (*Cai-shu-shi*).
"Great" (*Dà*) is the Chinese translation for the Indic term.
Therefore, the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra* states that Mahā-Śaivalī and Mahā-Kātyāyana composed the *Prajñapti-pāda-śāstra*.
It consists of eighteen thousand verses; "Kātyā" is translated here as "shearer."
"Yan" (衍) here means "lineage" (種).
"Na" (那) is a masculine sound;
it is one of the clans among the Brahmins. The above are the three treatises.
It was composed during the Buddha's lifetime;
[it was also compiled] within the first hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa by Devaśarman.
He composed the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* in seven thousand stanzas;
this [master] was Devaśarman, who lived until the beginning of the third century.
Vāsumitra [lived thereafter].
He composed the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* in six thousand stanzas,
which is the old *Saṅgītiparyāya-abhidharma*. He also composed the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*,
the extensive version of which consists of six thousand stanzas.
The *Abhidharmasamaya-prakaraṇa-śāstra* (abbreviated as *Samaya*) in seven hundred stanzas was composed by Vasumitra—here translated as "World Friend.
This is not the same Vasumitra who participated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā* assembly;
they share the same name but are distinct individuals. This occurred toward the end of the third century.
Kātyāyanīputra composed the Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra in twenty-five thousand stanzas.
Later reciters differed regarding the extent [of the text].
One version consists of eighteen thousand verses, while another consists of sixteen thousand verses;
this present version is that which was translated by the Master of He (Xuanzang). In the former six treatises, the categories of meaning are somewhat fewer.
The *Jñānaprasthāna* is the most extensive among the treatises on the Dharma-gates;
therefore, later masters of the treatises say that these six [treatises] are sufficient, with the *Jñānaprasthāna* serving as the body. These are the seven treatises mentioned above.
This is the fundamental treatise of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Upādhyāya,
only the *Prajñaptipāda-śāstra* remains untranslated.
The other six treatises have all been translated.
As for the explanation of this name— why it is called *Abhidharma*—
this is the explanation of the term *Abhidharma*.
First, the explanation of *dharma*;
second, the explanation of its correspondence. Regarding the explanation of the term *dharma*, there are two aspects: first, that which maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This means that all phenomena each maintain their respective intrinsic natures.
Just as the nature of form and so forth is eternally unchanging,
one generates a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the two modes [of existence].
Just as impermanence and so forth give rise to the human understanding of impermanence and so forth— this passage explains it for now by way of that which sustains [the object].
The [explanation of] "arising from the path" (*mārga-ja*) has been omitted for brevity;

its meaning should likewise be understood, or it may be implied. Regarding the term *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic): because its nature (*svabhāva*) is able to maintain its own essence, it is called a *dharma*. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Within a single entity, there is a distinction between its nature (*svabhāva*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):
in relation to its own name, it is called "nature";
in relation to other conditions, it is called "characteristic."
In terms of its meaning, "nature" (svabhāva) is defined as that which can maintain its characteristics (lakṣaṇa). Regarding the various treatises that state it can maintain its own nature,
there are briefly two different types of dharmas in which the characteristic can maintain the nature.
First, the dharma of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dharma*);
second, the dharma of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*). If the dharma of ultimate reality refers exclusively to the fruit of nirvāṇa, it is called "ultimate" because it is virtuous and permanent.
Because it possesses substantial reality, it is called "meaning" (*artha*);
that is, it is the supreme meaning.
Because it is the supreme meaning, it is called "dharma."
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
"Nirvāṇa" is here translated as "perfect quiescence. If the dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) pertain to the objects of the four truths, then the dharma-characteristics are termed "dharma."
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. According to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇadharma*), it is called "dharma" because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
this also applies to space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Because these two types are not subsumed under the Truths,
are not subsumed under the fruits [of the path],
and do not serve as objects for untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna).
This is not explained here [as such]. It is called "conducive" (*abhimukha*) because it is a dharma that can be directed toward the fruit of nirvāṇa;
that is, the cause is directed toward the fruit.

"Tending toward" refers to what is desired by the cause, which is called the fruit. Alternatively, it is explained in terms of the nature of cause and the nature of fruit: namely, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is the true "conducive" factor.
The remaining [paths], such as those of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and so forth, are called "converging" (*abhimukha*) because they give rise to the true converging [path].
Although the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) are not termed "converging" with respect to their own respective categories,
they are nonetheless termed "converging" with respect to what is subsequently realized, or with respect to *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
The four paths are all called "confronting" (*pratipannaka*).

Another interpretation holds that the contaminated wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) which is able to partially sever the afflictions is also called "confronting," while other types of wisdom, such as the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), are called "confronting" because they can give rise to that [wisdom] which confronts [the afflictions]. Yet another interpretation holds:
Because the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is superior during the state of mental scattering, it is also called "confronting" (*abhimukha*);

furthermore, because other forms of wisdom, such as that born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), are able to produce this confronting state, they too are called "confronting. Another interpretation holds that when the wholesome stage of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the wisdom born of hearing occurs, [it is so designated].
It is also called "confrontation" (*abhimukha*).

Because the wisdom acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) and other types [of wisdom] can produce confrontation, it is named "confrontation. Another explanation is that it refers to the wisdom acquired at birth.
Because it is able to discern the path leading toward nirvana, it is also called "oriented" (*abhimukha*);
because the proponent can generate that which is oriented, it is called "oriented.
Furthermore, it is explained as all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and contaminated (*sāsrava*) wisdoms and so forth.

And all such treatises have the power and capacity to be directed toward nirvāṇa; thus, all dharmas that constitute the fruit of the ultimate truth are called "directed. Alternatively, they are called "contemplative" because they are able to contemplate the objects of the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding the mind confronting its object:
untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is true confrontation and contemplation;
other forms of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and so forth give rise to true confrontation and contemplation.
Therefore, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Alternatively, it may be "confronting" (*abhimukha*) rather than "contemplation.
Another interpretation holds that because the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is able to contemplate the truths (*satya*), it is also termed "contemplation."
Other forms of wisdom, such as that derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), are also called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) because they can give rise to contemplative observation;

alternatively, they may be "oriented toward" [the truth] but not yet constitute full contemplation. Furthermore, it is explained that wisdom derived from reflection, when practiced during the state of mental scattering (*vikṣepa-avasthā*) with the superior intent to train in contemplating the truths, is also termed "contemplation of the truths" (*satya-vipaśyanā*).

Other forms of wisdom, such as the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), are called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) because they can give rise to it; alternatively, some are directed toward it but are not themselves contemplation.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the wholesome preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the wisdom derived from hearing, which is subsumed under the training in the superior contemplation of the truths (*satya-vipaśyanā-śikṣā*), is also termed "contemplation."
The wisdom acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) and so forth are called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) because they can produce contemplation;
alternatively, they may be "oriented toward" (*abhimukha*) [the truths] but not themselves "contemplation.

Another interpretation holds that the wisdom acquired at birth is also called "contemplation" because it can differentiate and contemplate the truths. Furthermore, the scriptural teachings are called "contemplation" because they can produce contemplation.
Alternatively, it may be directed toward [an object] rather than being contemplative (*vipaśyanā*). Furthermore,
it is explained as all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and contaminated (*sāsrava*) wisdoms (*prajñā*),
as well as various treatises (*śāstra*).
Because all [these treatises] have the power and capacity to contemplate the truths directly (*abhimukha*), they are all termed "contemplation" (*abhimukha*). Therefore, they are called *Abhidharma*.
This concludes the section;
it should be understood thus.
Among these, that which is capable of confronting [an object] and which confronts [it] preeminently is,
for the time being, given the name "confrontation" (*pratigha*).
Speaking in terms of ultimate reality, it is also called "dharma" because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
as for that which is confronted,
the dharma is superior.
Furthermore, they are given names according to the Dharma;

in reality, they are also called "counterparts" because they are that which is countered. Alternatively, each side is mentioned individually as a shorthand, with one implying the other; or it is based on the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.

This means that because it is the counter-correlative of a phenomenon (*dharma*), that which can act as the counter-correlative is called the "counter-correlative" (*pratipakṣa*); that which is the object of the counter-correlation is called the "phenomenon.
This is based on either the possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) or the appositional compound (*karmadhāraya*).
Both the subject and the object are termed Abhidharma.
By this analogy, it should be understood that the Four Noble Truths are termed the Abhidharma of Principle (nyāyābhidharma).
Nirvāṇa is called the "fruit" (phala) of the Abhidharma (dharma).
The root verse mentions only the "counteragent" (pratipakṣa),
which is why the principle of the fruit is not explicitly stated.
The prose passage mentions both the agent and the object;
for this reason, it also speaks of "principle" (*nyāya*) and "fruit" (*phala*).
Alternatively, it may be understood as an implicit indication. Question: Why is it called *Abhidharma* (the "Higher Dharma") and not *Abhivastu* (the "Higher Entity")?
If one follows the Sanskrit pronunciation,
why is it called *abhidharma* and not *abhidharmma*?
The explanation is that "dharma" refers to the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
There is a pervasive superior resolve regarding the fact that all phenomena possess their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa),
which ordinary beings and noble ones alike constantly take as their object.
Because no such conviction arises,
it is said that "Abhidharma" (the Dharma of Abhi) does not refer to "the Dharma of existing things" (dharmāṇām abhidharmam).
Nevertheless, the treatise provisionally explains "Dharma" in terms of its capacity to uphold [the teachings].

This dharma is the dharma of dharmas, as explained in detail within the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic). Taking this opportunity, I shall briefly clarify the different ways in which the *Abhidharma* is categorized and synthesized.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the explicit explanation of the opening and closing;
second, a brief explanation of the names.
Regarding the explicit explanation of the opening and closing:
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, clarifying the increase according to number;
second, clarifying the gradual increase.
Within the progressive increase of the enumerations, there are further four types:
namely, (1) one type as one, (2) two types as two, (3) three types as three, and (4) four types as four. Regarding "one type as one":
Regarding the statement that the Abhidharma takes all phenomena as its essence, yet the various treatises do not mention space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*):
this is because these two are not included within the [Four] Truths.
Because it is not subsumed under the category of fruit,
and because it does not serve as an object for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). Regarding the statement "two kinds,
two," the first two [verses] say:
First, the ultimate Abhidharma,
which refers to the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha).
Second, the conventional Abhidharma.
That is to say, the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ*).
Since these two are both capable of being counteracted (*pratipakṣa*), they are called "counter-factors" (*abhidharma*).
As this treatise states: "The second 'two'..."
First, the Abhidharma of objects;
"objects" refers to the objects of the Four Truths.
Second, the Abhidharma of fruits.
The fruit refers to nirvāṇa.
These two are both the phenomena that are "countered";
thus they are called Abhidharma.
This treatise also speaks of three kinds of "three.
Regarding the first set of three, it says:
first, the Abhidharma of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It refers to untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) and,
secondly, the Abhidharma that accompanies it,
which refers to all dharmas associated with and co-existent with that wisdom.
The third is the Abhidharma of the equipment,
which has as its essence the four types of contaminated wisdom along with their concomitants,
as well as the various treatises.
As stated in this treatise, the second and third [sections] say:
first, the ultimate Abhidharma;
second, the conventional Abhidharma.
The three *dharmas* that serve as the objects of opposition are all as previously explained.
Regarding the third triad, it says:
First, the Abhidharma of the object; second, the Abhidharma of the fruit; third, the Abhidharma of the means of investigation.
These are also as previously explained. Regarding the four sets of four: as for the first set of four, it is said:
First, the Abhidharma of the Teaching.
"Teaching" refers to the instructional discourse;
