What are the two cessations of space? This is the question regarding enumeration.
Regarding the distinction between cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation:
the answer is that these states, such as the attainment of space (*ākāśa-samāpatti*), are designated as untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
The fetters of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). Why is this so?
This is the inquiry.
Regarding the phrase "because the various outflows do not increase therein," the answer is:
the various outflows.
Because they do not increase [in strength] within those untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
That is to say, the nature of untainted phenomena is contrary to the outflows (āsrava).
They certainly cannot be associated with the outflows (*āsrava*) such that they could serve as their objects;
however, because their natures are mutually contradictory and they do not increase together,
they cannot be designated as "with-outflow" (*sāsrava*) in relation to the outflows.
If it is the truth of cessation or the truth of the path,
they do not increase by way of being objects;
this is also the case for space and analytical cessation.
It is neither a condition nor does it increase [afflictions].
Regarding the brief explanation that extends up to form,
herein one should also clarify the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārga-āryasatya*).
The nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) will not be explained here, as it is explained extensively in the subsequent text.
If its substantial entities were distinguished according to their individual instances, they would be numerous;
however, for now, three are designated in general.
Therefore, it is said in brief that space has non-obstruction alone as its intrinsic nature,
because it accommodates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Although the aforementioned treatise states that space accommodates conditioned phenomena such as form, it further asserts that the essential nature of space cannot be said to exist here or there,
because it lacks spatial location.
Just as with visual consciousness and so forth— Question: If it is called "space" because it does not obstruct,
then the nature of matter (rūpa) within the space-element (ākāśadhātu) also does not obstruct others.
It should be named "empty space" (*ākāśa*).
The commentary explains:
it is the matter of the element of space (*ākāśadhātu-rūpa*).
Although its nature is not that of an obstructer,
it is nonetheless that which is obstructed;
for it is displaced and avoided when hindered by other forms of matter.
Its essence is non-arising.
What the world calls "space" is the designation of the term "space" applied to the matter of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*). If that is so, [then...]
If non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) were not capable of being obstructed or of obstructing others, it should be called space (*ākāśa*).
The explanation says:
because it arises from that which is obstructed, it is not a valid analogy. If that were so, [what of] the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*)?
The two types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth are neither the obstructing agent nor the obstructed object,
nor do they give rise to obstruction.
It should be named "empty space.
The commentary states:
According to this aspect of its meaning, it is likewise identical to empty space.
Established as a distinct name,
space has non-obstruction alone as its intrinsic nature; thus,
although it is designated by a general term, it receives this specific name.
Just as with the sense-base of form and so forth,
because space is unobstructed, both the primary elements and the derived forms [can exist].
Movement occurs therein;
since abiding in reality and so forth also depend upon space, movement is explained in terms of manifestation.
Alternatively, "movement" refers to arising.
Regarding the statement that "form arises therein," another interpretation is that since space has no location or spatial dimension,
it cannot be said that form moves within it.
As for the practitioner,
they move within the form of the space-element;
furthermore, the space-element exists by virtue of empty space.
In this context, space is explained;
yet, when it is called "matter of the space-element" (ākāśa-dhātu-rūpa), the coarse is used to manifest the subtle. Question:
Since the essence of space itself is non-obstructive and formless, why is it said that matter moves within it?
The commentary states:
"In principle, space is likewise not obstructed by formlessness."
Because it is manifested through material form (*rūpa*), it is explained specifically [as such]. Question:
Since formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*) also possess the nature of non-obstruction, why is it said that space does not obstruct the formless?
The commentary states:
Formless conditioned phenomena are capable of performing functions.
Space is called "unobstructed" because it does not hinder;
cessation through deliberation is called "cessation through deliberation" because it is attained through deliberation.
This explains the essential nature of cessation through deliberation.
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) has the nature of dissociation (visamyoga). What is dissociation?
It is the separation of all contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) from their two types of bondage: those consisting of association (saṃprayoga) and those consisting of objects (ālambana).
And one is able to realize liberation and nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, the essence of that cessation is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because it is manifested by the dissociation [from defilements]. Question: If one realizes cessation through deliberation by being dissociated from fetters, then consider a case where the knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen.

Even when [a factor] is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), it remains bound by the pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) of the lower realm belonging to the origin (*samudaya*).
How, then, can one realize cessation? There are nine grades in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
If one has abandoned from the first grade up to the eighth grade,
yet remains bound by the subsequent grade,
how can one realize cessation?
The commentary says:
Although that which binds has been severed,
that which is bound is liberated.
One realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
However, the afflictions that act as bonds are of varying strengths.
First is the bond of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*), which refers to the various afflictions binding the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that arise simultaneously with them.
Second is the bondage of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This refers to the poisonous power of the afflictions (*kleśa*) directed toward an object;
it binds that object so that one does not attain mastery over it.
Within the context of conditions and fetters, there are further four types:
first, those of the same category and the same class;
second, those of the same category but different classes.
Third, the same category within a different class;
fourth, a different category within a different class.
Together with the preceding "correspondence," there are five bonds in total.
Among the five fetters (*pañca-bandhanāni*), those that are severed through direct realization (*sākṣāt-kriyā*) are strong;
those severed without such realization are weak. Regarding "strong" and "weak":
first, the fetter of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) is the strongest in its power.
Second, those bound by the same category and the same type have a binding force that is next strongest;
third, those bound by the same category but a different type have a binding force that is next strongest;
fourth, those bound by a different category but the same type have a binding force that is somewhat weaker.
Among the five types of bonds of differing categories and differing natures, their power is weakest; among these five bonds,
the first three are strong and the latter two are weak.
If one abandons the first three [categories], one realizes their respective analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as appropriate;
however, for the latter two types, the power of their bondage is weak, and thus analytical cessation is not realized by means of abandoning them.
This is just as, in the case of phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), there are generally two kinds.
Associated phenomena constitute one category;
acquisition and the four characteristics constitute another category.
Associated phenomena possess five fetters.

There are four remaining bonds associated with the four characteristics. If the knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, then there are the factors associated with what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
This is because of the severing of the bonds associated with it,
the bonds of the same category and same grade,
and the bonds of the same category but different grades.
Because the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is through the power of abandonment,
it is associated with the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
this is due to the abandonment of factors belonging to the same category and the same class.
Because they are bound by the same category but different classes,
one realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
this is because their abandonment is more powerful, and thus these associated phenomena [are abandoned].
This includes the attainment [of cessation] and its four characteristics.
At that time, although one has bound the pervasive afflictions of the lower realms, the same category, and different categories through their accumulation,
because these are subtle and weak, one realizes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, even if at that time one has severed the bonds of the latter four categories—
namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) across different classes (nikāya) but within the same or different types (sajāti/vijāti)—
one is still unable to realize the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of those latter four categories.
Because that which is not yet abandoned is still powerful, the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) are abandoned collectively, one grade at a time, out of the nine grades;
this is because the afflictions to be abandoned are categorized into nine grades.
Therefore, it can be said that there are "similar grades" and "dissimilar grades," as is the case with those abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-heya).
Those abandoned through the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path each consist of two categories;
this may be understood by analogy with the preceding explanation. Those abandoned through the path of cultivation consist of three categories in total.
Dharmas associated with defilement constitute one category;
the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) acquired regarding those dharmas associated with defilement constitute another category;
and all other contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas constitute yet another category.
This refers to defiled matter (*rūpa*),
along with the acquisition (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertaining to that matter,
as well as the five non-defiled aggregates (*skandha*). The first category is endowed with all five fetters (*bandhana*).
The latter two categories each have four types of bonds (*bandhana*).

The bond of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*) is excluded because it does not consist of association with afflictions (*kleśa*). When one abandons the first category of defiled associated dharmas, it is by means of abandoning the bond of association.
One is bound by the fetters of the same category and the same type;
because the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has severed the predominant [fetters],
at that time, although one remains bound by the other eight types belonging to different categories within the same category.
Because they are weak, they also realize the unconditioned;
this is not the same as the path of seeing,
because on the path of seeing, each of the nine grades [of afflictions] is abandoned one by one.
Therefore, when the same category (*nikāya*) and the same grade (*prakāra*) are present, both [the same-grade and the different-grade] can be said to be strong.
In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the nine grades are abandoned separately;
therefore, when the same category is present but a different grade, it is designated as weak—or so it may be understood.
In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those belonging to the same category (*nikāya*) but different classes (*prakāra*) are also termed "weak.
This is like the various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who abandon the five categories in a mixed manner;
as they abandon each preceding class, [the subsequent ones are likewise weak].
It is still bound by the afflictions of the delusions of view;
because it is weak, it also realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
From this perspective, one knows that it is weak.
Since the pervasive afflictions belonging to other categories and to both the similar and dissimilar classes have already been abandoned,
even if those [remaining] were not abandoned, one would still realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
because their bondage is inferior. The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the first category of defilements possesses four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
When the first category is abandoned,
because the fetters of the same class and same category are abandoned,
it is due to the abandonment of the strongest [fetters].
One realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The same category with different aspects,
as well as different categories with the same or different aspects, are all explained according to the preceding interpretation.

As with the abandonment of the first category, the abandonment of the remaining eight categories can be understood by applying this same explanation. All other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena also consist of nine categories;
because they correspond in their respective analogies, they are described as being of the same or different categories.

When abandoning the remaining outflow-tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), one abandons the fetters (*bandhana*) belonging to the same category (*nikāya*) and the same or different grades (*prakāra*).
Because these are abandoned with particular force, one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
for the fetters belonging to other categories, whether of the same or different grades, have already been abandoned previously.
Even if one does not sever those [objects], one still realizes their analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because the bondage is inferior;
furthermore, these other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are bound by being objects of cognition.
To sever them, it is necessary to exhaustively sever all nine grades of the afflictions that take them as objects.
Only the objects of perception (*ālambana*) are called "abandoned. Question:

Since acquisition (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also bonds of perception, why is it that upon the abandonment of whichever category of afflictions (*kleśa*), that acquisition and those four characteristics likewise realize cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
The nine grades of afflictions can also give rise to material karma (*rūpa-karman*) of nine grades.
Why is it that the material karma thus produced does not undergo simultaneous abandonment,
realization, and cessation along with those afflictions?
The commentary states:
Although obtaining (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are indeed bound by conditions,
the four characteristics act as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) with respect to the afflictions.
Because they are thus related,
they share the same abandonment and the same realization;
although this attainment is not a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) with respect to the afflictions, it is nonetheless related to them as a direct cause.
Because there must be acquisition (*prāpti*) whenever these afflictions exist,
there is no instance where a bodily action (*rūpa-karman*) is produced while the affliction exists yet lacks acquisition.
Whether [the action] exists or not is indeterminate.
Although at the time of a material action there may also be the defilements capable of issuing it,
there may be this category of defilement without that material action,
as in the case of one who has already abandoned them.
Because they are remote due to delusion and error, one must sever the nine grades [of defilements] before attaining the realization of cessation. Question:
Just as with the severing of roots of goodness or the relinquishing of precepts, this precept is acquired in accordance with the arising of that wholesome mind.
If that mind is severed, this precept is then relinquished;
when the afflictions that give rise to physical action are severed, [the precept is likewise relinquished].
Why is it that the karma of form is not abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions?
The explanation states:
"Abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and "relinquishment" (*tyāga*) have distinct meanings.
This cannot be taken as a universal rule.
There are instances where there is abandonment through severance (*prahāṇa*) rather than relinquishment (*tyāga*),
such as when one severs tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the like.
There are instances of relinquishment that are not abandonment, such as the relinquishment of the prātimokṣa vows and so forth.
"Discernment" (pratisaṃkhyā) refers to analytical investigation; it is for this reason that this statement was made.

Explaining the term "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): it refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) which, being distinct from tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*), is called a "distinction of wisdom. Alternatively, it is that which is undefiled and distinct from the defiled, and is thus called a "distinction of wisdom. Because these distinct forms of wisdom individually and specifically discern the Four Noble Truths, the essence of cessation exists prior [to its actualization].
However, it is not accomplished [by that alone].

That which is obtained through the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is called cessation through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). That which is obtained through the power of mere absence is simply called cessation;
it is so termed because it is the cessation [brought about] by discernment.
It is named "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound,
just as a cart drawn by oxen is called an "ox-cart."
This statement is made by omitting certain intermediate terms;
the same applies to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the question, "Are all contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) identical in their analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)?",
the answer is: No.
Answer:
"What is it? This is an inquiry.
Regarding the statement, "If it were to reach [the state of disjunction] according to the distinctions of the objects of bondage, it would be useless":

this is explained as follows. That is to say, according to the quantity—whether many or few—of the objects of the various contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena that constitute bondage, the quantity of the objects of disjunction (*visamyoga*) is likewise [many or few]. If it were not so, [the path would be useless].
Furthermore, if you claim that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) share one and the same cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
then at the moment one realizes the cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
one should simultaneously realize the cessation of all afflictions to be abandoned across the five categories (*pañca-varga*).
If one were to realize it in this manner,
then cultivating the remedial paths that abandon the remaining four categories [of afflictions] would be rendered useless.
Because it has already been realized previously.
If one were to say that what was first realized is only a partial portion and not the whole,
then a single entity of cessation would necessarily possess multiple parts.
The notion that a single entity possesses multiple parts contradicts reason; therefore,
cessation conforms to its substratum,
as the entities are distinct and manifold.
However, when sentient beings realize that cessation,
although they give rise to distinct acquisitions (*prāpti*), they all realize it identically.
Based on what meaning is it said that cessation has no "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
Objection: Since the essence of cessation is manifold, there ought to be similar types [of cessation].
Based on what meaning does the Sūtra state that cessation has no similar type? [Response:
It is based on the fact that cessation itself is non-existent; it does not mean that there is no similar type.
Generally speaking, when dharmas are considered in relation to their own extinction-natures,
they certainly lack the status of being a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu),
nor do they serve as a homogeneous cause for others.
This distinguishes it from the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*). Therefore, that sūtra states as follows:
"It is not the case that cessation itself lacks multiple entities of the same kind. Having thus explained analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), [the text continues:]
Regarding "the attainment of non-analytical cessation which forever obstructs future arising":
this explains non-analytical cessation. It refers to a dharma-substance that is capable of forever obstructing the arising of future dharmas.
This fundamental dharma intends to obstruct the arising of dharmas so that they do not arise.
If a dharma does not arise, then "attainment" (prāpti) arises and is bestowed upon the practitioner;
therefore, it is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-prāpti*). This prior cessation is wholesome.
Because it is subsequently extinguished by the indeterminate, it is said to be "different from the former"; this is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This concludes the definition of its essence. It is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because it is attained by means of deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
That which is attained not through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*) but solely by the absence of conditions is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is the explanation of its name. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained by means of deliberation;
cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained by the deficiency of conditions.
Therefore, it is said that the attainment of cessation differs from the former. For example, when the eye and mental consciousness are in continuous succession, focusing exclusively on a single form.
By mentioning the eye, the eye-consciousness is already included,
because whenever there is the seeing of forms, consciousness necessarily exists. Alternatively, what is called "mind" (manas) refers to the eye-consciousness.
It is also called "mind" (*manas*) among the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Alternatively,
what is called "mind" refers to the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*),
because all seven elements of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) are designated as "mind."
If one adopts this interpretation, it fully encompasses both the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*);

for while the visual consciousness is simultaneous [with its object], the mental consciousness occurs before and after it. Furthermore, other objects such as form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibles may have already passed away.
The five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and so forth that would have taken those objects as their conditions shall abide in the future and never arise at all;
this is because the five groups of sensory consciousnesses and so forth are incapable of taking those past objects as their conditions.

Because the conditions are not complete, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Among the factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and the inclusion of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*),
there are those that serve as objects simultaneously with their corresponding cognitive faculties (*ālambaka*),
such as the objects of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and so forth, as well as the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).

This includes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth, because it also takes simultaneous objects as its conditions, just like the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the like. Question: When a dharma has not yet arisen...
"If it is merely due to the absence of conditions,
what does this have to do with cessation?
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xianzong lun) answers:
It is not the case that [a phenomenon] will never arise again simply because its conditions were lacking;
for when it later encounters conditions of a similar kind, it should arise once more.
That is to say, even if the conditions were previously absent...
One might ask: "How can that dharma not arise?
Later, when it encounters conditions of its own kind, what obstacle prevents it from arising? To this, the commentary explains:
the intention of that treatise is as follows.
It should be understood that the non-arising of this dharma is not caused solely by the deficiency of conditions; it also occurs because of its cessation (*nirodha*).
This cessation, in terms of its acquisition (*prāpti*), is specifically designated as "non-arising."
In terms of its substantial nature, it actually pervades the three periods of time and is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, states that the proponents of the definitive view (*viniścayavādin*) say:
"Non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has a numerical quantity equal to that of conditioned phenomena."
The analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) corresponds in number to the quantity of contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma).

Since that treatise states it corresponds to the quantity of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), and since past, present, and future-to-be-born phenomena are included within the category of the conditioned.
It should be understood accordingly that those phenomena possess non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one were to say they do not, [it would contradict the following].
If this essence is unarisen, there should be no cessation of it.
If one says that this cessation exists precisely because it is unarisen,
then this cessation would possess an inherent nature.
It must therefore be impermanent.
If one says that the natures of produced and unproduced phenomena are each fixed,
then produced phenomena would simply not exist.
Since that which is unarisen exists,
the treatise should not employ the phrase "lacking conditions" when speaking of permanence.
Moreover, if that were the case,
the cultivation of the path would be useless;
this is proven by such reasoning.
Therefore, it generally pertains to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
There are many further passages that cannot be cited here in full. Question:
Regarding this non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), do all classes of sentient beings attain it collectively?
Is it not acquired in common?
The explanation says:
It refers to the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding external, insentient, and commonly shared phenomena.
It is attained by all together,
because it is produced by the collective karma of sentient beings.
This refers to the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding internal phenomena that are not shared among sentient beings.
They are each acquired individually,
because sentient beings are moved by their respective karmas. Thus,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, states:
This non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is not fixed:
with respect to shared dharmas, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained collectively;
with respect to unshared dharmas, non-analytical cessation is attained individually. Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
External insentient phenomena and the visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles within the bodies of others are all capable of being enjoyed in common because their characteristics are manifest;
if these lack the necessary conditions, they arise simultaneously for all.
The five faculties, as well as the mind and its mental objects (citta-caitta-dharma), have distinct functions that are concealed by their characteristics.
If these lack their respective conditions, they each attain [their results] separately. Furthermore, it is explained thus:
All internal and external phenomena,
which should be enjoyed in common by as many sentient beings as appropriate,
do not arise individually.
When it is appropriate for a certain number of sentient beings to experience [an attainment] together,
there arises an "attainment-of-attainment" (prāpti-prāpti);
this is called "common attainment" (sādhāraṇa-prāpti).
If it were intended solely for one's own enjoyment,
this dharma would not arise; rather,
it would merely be attained through one's own effort.
The names are each obtained separately.

Regarding the statement that "the obtainment of cessation with respect to dharmas extends to past, present, and future produced dharmas," this clarifies the fourfold distinction of the obtainment of the two types of cessation (*nirodha*). Since space (*ākāśa*) is not an obtainment, it is not treated here for comparison.
The reasons why there is no attainment are explained separately below:
namely, past, present, and future dharmas,
as well as dharmas that do not arise.
These are said to each have both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
Two sets of four constitute eight. In the first phrase there are three factors:
namely, all outflowing phenomena of the past, present, and future.
Because they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they attain cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because they are past, present, or destined to arise, they do not attain cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The second phrase consists of one dharma.
This refers to unarisen dharmas that are untainted (anāsrava) and conditioned (saṃskṛta).
Because they do not arise, they attain cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha);
because they are untainted, they do not attain cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
By means of "outflow-free" (anāsrava), one distinguishes from "with-outflows" (sāsrava);
by means of "conditioned" (saṃskṛta), one distinguishes from "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta). In the third phrase, there is one dharma:
namely, those non-arisen dharmas that are with-outflows.
Because they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), one attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because they do not arise, one attains cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The fourth phrase consists of three categories of phenomena:
namely, all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena of the past, present, and those destined to arise.

because they are past, present, or arising phenomena, they cannot attain cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Thus has been explained to what extent something is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).

Because it is produced through the collective action of various conditions assembled according to their respective requirements, it is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
There is certainly no phenomenon whatsoever that is produced by a single condition alone. [This is stated] to suppress the following objection:
Past and present phenomena, being produced by a multitude of conditions, can be designated as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Since future phenomena have not yet been produced,
how can they be called conditioned?
Therefore, it is now stated generally:
this is a fault of theirs, because it is of the same category as existing conditioned phenomena;
thus it is also called "conditioned."
There is no contradiction regarding the future,
just as when a child drinks milk,
that which is in the breast is also called milk.
Because it is of the same nature as that which flows [into the fire],
that which is currently burning is called fuel,
and that which has not yet burned is also called fuel.
Because it consumes its own kind.
As for the statement that "these conditioned phenomena reach the point of being swallowed up," these conditioned phenomena are also called "worldly paths."
That is to say, conditioned phenomena proceed within this world:
past phenomena are of the nature of having already proceeded,
and present phenomena are of the nature of currently proceeding.
Future phenomena possess the nature of being about to arise;
since all unarisen phenomena belong to that same category,
there is no error in establishing this designation.
Because the world (*loka*) is the path (*mārga*), it is called the "world-path" (*lokamārga*).
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive determinative).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Because the five aggregates, such as form, are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing,
they circulate through the paths of the future, present, and past; furthermore,

It is established according to the Dharma.
The Dharma is that upon which the world relies; it is called the "path.

The present dharma is the nature of the world’s current practice;
the future dharma is the nature of the world’s future practice.
Because it is the path of the world, it is called the "world-path."
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). The four characteristics of impermanence are that which devours;
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are that which is devoured.
Because these phenomena that are devoured are subject to destruction, they are called "worldly" (*loka*).
Because it is the locus of impermanence, it is called a "path" (*adhvan*).

Therefore, Master Paramārtha said:
The road is consumed by walking;
it is like a road ten thousand *li* long,
which is traversed step by step without ceasing.

so too it is with the five aggregates;
because they are subject to impermanence, they ultimately perish and are extinguished.
Regarding the statement that "the basis of designation (nāma-adhiṣṭhāna) is subsumed within the eighteen elements":
these conditioned phenomena are also the basis of designation. "Designation" refers to speech, which has sound as its essence.
The basis upon which speech relies consists of names and meanings,
for speech functions by depending on names and meanings. Regarding "names together with their meanings":
This refers to both the name and its referent.
Regarding the meaning of their co-occurrence throughout the three periods of time,
within these three periods, the name may sometimes precede the referent and sometimes follow it.
In some cases, the name follows the meaning;
in others, the name and the meaning are simultaneous.
Whether the designator and the designated are identical or different, [the relationship remains].
Since both [the name and the object] equally fall within the worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*), they can both be said to be "together.
This is because, in relation to the speech that expresses them,
both the name and the object equally fall within the worldly convention and possess a direct utility.
Therefore, because this [unconditioned] is the basis for speech,
and since the unconditioned is a phenomenon transcending the world,
it is useless and remote in relation to the speech capable of describing it.

it is said that while [the name] can express meaning, it is not the basis for speech. Furthermore,
another explanation is that "name" is as previously described.
Regarding the meaning of "together" (*saha*):
it means that both the meaning and the word fall together into the world of conventional usage.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "together" refers to both the name (*nāman*) and the meaning (*artha*).
That is to say: both the name and the object; both the name and the meaning.
This refers to the name and the meaning.
It is because it coexists with speech;
for whether it be the meaning or the name,
they can both be spoken together.
Because they fall together into the world,
they are called "conjoined" (*sahabhū*). Regarding the names and meanings,
when compared with the words [of the sūtras], their similarities and differences across the three periods of time are as follows.
It should be explained accordingly that they are both present.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (Taishō 1546), fascicle 15, states:
"The Venerable Pārśva said:"
Conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) can coexist with verbal expression; therefore,

The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is not so.
Therefore, the treatise does not state that [the aforementioned] "basis" (āśraya) encompasses all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma).
Otherwise, [it would be redundant].
However, they merely hold that the name is the basis of expression (*vāgvastu*) as its substance;
this contradicts the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*,
which states that the basis of expression is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).
Question: As the *Nyāyānusāra* quotes the *Prakaraṇapāda*, saying, "By this, one correctly understands the *Prakaraṇapāda*;
it states that [the basis] is comprised within the five aggregates."
Why do the citations in the two treatises differ?

Because it is explained in full in the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā* (Vibhāṣā XV).
Thus, that treatise says:
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the basis of speech (*vāg-āśraya*)?
Answer: The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states that the basis of speech consists of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The twelve bases (āyatana) are subsumed within the five aggregates (skandha). Furthermore,
it is explained that this treatise is intended to refute the exclusive attachment to the view that the name-base (nāma-āyatana) alone constitutes the essence [of consciousness].

The *Nyāyānusāra* specifically cites the passage on the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) because it aims to refute the position that the basis (*āśraya*) also extends to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It specifically cites the passage on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) for the same reason.

Each [position] cites its own side, and there is no contradiction or harm [in this]. Question: According to one explanation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, "name" (*nāman*) is the basis for speech, while "meaning" (*artha*)—
This statement refers to mutual dependence.

Since there are these two masters, [the following discussion arises].
Regarding this treatise’s statement on "basis" (āśraya), with what is it identical?
To explain:

there is no contradiction in either case.

Explanation: It is said that names are manifested as reflections.

Regarding the statement, "Or it is called 'possessing departure' because there is departure from that existence," these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are also called "possessing departure."
"Detachment" means eternal detachment;
it is precisely nirvāṇa.
By means of this nirvāṇa, one is able to eternally abandon and detach from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Because all conditioned phenomena are characterized by their departure from that [conditioned state],
just as one who possesses wealth is called "wealthy," so too is the Noble Path like a boat or raft.
One should likewise relinquish them.
As a sutra says:
"Even phenomena should be relinquished."
How much more so for that which is non-dharmic?
Or, what is called "that which has an object" (sālambana) refers to those things transmitted as being such;
these conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are also called "having an object."
"Thing" (*vastu*) has the meaning of "cause.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise from causes, they are called "possessing things" (*savastuka*). This is the Sautrāntika interpretation.
Phenomena (dharma) are the substance.
Conditioned phenomena possess substance;
unconditioned phenomena lack substance. The intention of the Master [Vasubandhu] aligns with the Sautrāntika school.
Because one does not believe in the causes and conditions of things,
it is said that "it is thus transmitted by tradition. The phrase "such categories as these, up to the various specific names," serves as the conclusion.
Regarding the phrase "the three realms of existence, etc., up to the aforementioned 'places of view'" (*yathokta-dṛṣṭisthāna-tri-bhava-ādi*):
the following section secondly clarifies the various names for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This line cites the preceding verse. The term "etc. (*ādi*) means that it includes the four categories beginning with "that which is defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*).
The Commentary says: "What is established here?
This is the question. Regarding these contaminated [phenomena], what further is established?
It means that the "aggregates of clinging" are established, up to the description of them as being like trees with flowers and fruit.
Answer: Regarding these contaminated [phenomena], they are established as the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).

These aggregates of grasping are not only called "aggregates of grasping," but are also called simply "aggregates" (*skandha*). Alternatively, there may be those that are merely aggregates but are not aggregates of grasping.
This refers to untainted (anāsrava) formations.

Because the term "aggregate" (skandha) is used generically, just as fire produced from grass and chaff is called "grass-chaff fire," the aggregates produced from grasping (upādāna) are called "aggregates of grasping" (upādānaskandha).
It is named according to its cause;
"grasping" (*upādāna*) refers to the afflictions because they are capable of grasping.
This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
A subject belonging to a king is called a "king's subject.
Because the aggregates (skandhas) belong to grasping (upādāna), they are called "aggregates of grasping" (upādānaskandha).
This is a designation based on that to which something belongs: a tree from which flowers and fruits grow is called a "flower-fruit tree."
The aggregates are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*) because they can produce clinging;
this is a designation based on their result.
These contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are like those that possess outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because afflictions (*kleśa*) are discordant, they are designated by the term "contention" (*raṇa*). They stir up what is wholesome and cause harm to oneself and others;
this explains the etymology of "contention.
Because contention increases and persists therein, it is called "possessing contention" (*saraṇa*).
Just as it was previously stated that they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because the outflows increase therein,
this same explanation applies to what is "with conflict" (*saraṇa*).
Furthermore, they are also called "suffering" (*duḥkha*) because they contradict the minds of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
These contaminated phenomena are also called suffering;
they are the flowing and impermanent fruits of contaminated suffering,
yet ordinary beings do not perceive this.
The Noble Ones loathe it;
therefore, it is said that it merely contradicts the Noble Ones' minds.
Furthermore, it is called "origination" because it is capable of summoning suffering.
These contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are also called "origination" (*samudaya*),
because they summon the fruit of suffering;
they are also called "the world" (*loka*), because they reach up to the point where an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) arises.
These contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are also called "mundane" (*loka*) because they are subject to destruction;
they are distinguished from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because they possess antidotes (*pratipakṣa*),
and they are distinguished from the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Regarding the phrase "also called the locus of views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein":
these contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are also called the locus of views.
"Views" refers to the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*).

Because it is observed that [ignorance] dwells within tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and conforms to and increases the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), its mode of activity being subtle, it is described as "sleep" (*middha*).
Question: Among the outflows (*āsrava*), graspings (*upādāna*), and disputes (*raṇa*), views (*dṛṣṭi*) are also included.
The various afflictions, such as greed and so forth, also increase accordingly;
why, then, are the five views specifically singled out here?
The explanation is as follows:
Based on the establishment and rejection [of categories] in the four gates of the *Nyāyānusāra*, there are two:
first, all aspects (*sarvākāra*);
second, all times (*sarvakāla*).
Third, there is no differentiation;
fourth, firm adherence and immovability.
The commentary says:
That treatise states:
"To universally take the five categories as objects is called 'all modes' (*sarvākāra*);
alternatively, to universally take the six objects as objects is called 'all modes. To arise spontaneously is called 'all times' (*sarvadā*)."

Whether toward the agreeable or the disagreeable, to arise with equanimity is called "at all times"; to have no distinct characteristics in its essence is called "undifferentiated"; to be firm and unshakable in grasping objects is called "firmly fixed and immovable. [These pertain to] the three: greed, hatred, and pride.
Although it is called "all aspects" because it takes the five categories or the six objects as its conditions,
it does not [arise] at all times,
for it arises only when encountering the necessary conditions.
Alternatively, greed and pride arise when encountering what is agreeable,
while hatred arises when encountering what is disagreeable;
since these do not occur at all times, they are not present in every instance.
Although ignorance is not without differentiation at all times—
because there is a distinction between that which is independent and that which is associated—
it is said that it is "not without differentiation. Although doubt is without such [independent] differentiation...
Yet they are not rigidly fixed or immovable; it is only these five views that possess all four meanings.
They are specifically designated as "strong" because they also encompass the three realms of existence and are subsumed within the three realms of existence.
These contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are also called the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
The three realms of existence are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
They serve as the cause for these three realms of existence.
The cause is precisely the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*);
it serves as the basis for the three conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
That which is the basis is precisely the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Furthermore, because they are subsumed within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*),

and by virtue of possessing these three meanings, they are called the "three existences" (*tribhava*). This concludes the section on such categories up to the specific names according to their respective meanings.

This constitutes the first explanation of the five sense faculties.
It concludes the preceding discussion and raises a new inquiry.
The verse states: "That which reaches [objects] is called the five faculties, such as the eye.
The verse answers by stating: "They are the pure matter upon which those consciousnesses depend.
The five principles [of this] mean:
The former [term] "basis of that consciousness" excludes the four faculties such as the ear;
the latter term "pure matter" (rūpa-prasāda) [excludes the other types of matter].
To exclude the mind that has just ceased without interval (*anantara-niruddha*). Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"The former term indicates the eye of the same class (*sabhāga*), while the latter term indicates the eye of the same class that is not currently functioning (*tatsabhāga*). Another interpretation is as follows.
Visible form (rūpa) pervades eleven bases (āyatana).
"Based on" serves to distinguish it from its objects;
"based on" here refers to the six sense faculties (indriya).
The term "pure" (*śuddha*) excludes the five sense faculties and includes faith (*śraddhā*).
The term "form" (*rūpa*) excludes faith. Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
If that consciousness possesses a pure matter as its support, it is then designated as the "eye" and so forth;
if there is any deficiency, it is not so designated.
If one were to speak of it merely as the support for that consciousness...
It does not speak of "pure matter" (anāsrava-rūpa),
as that would conflate it with the equal-and-immediate support (samanantara-āśraya),
since the five consciousnesses also take the mind (manas) as their support.
Therefore, the first chapter of the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra* states:
"The claim that consciousness alone relies [on the sense organs] is confused with the immediate mind (*anantara-manas*).
It merely says that the five pure material bodies (*rūpa*) should be identical."
Therefore, the term "pure matter" (*rūpa-prasāda*) is used to exclude the [four] bases that are immediately contiguous.

The phrase "serving as the support for the eye-consciousness and so forth" indicates that there are five distinct types of sense faculties, such as the eye. If the treatise had merely said "the purity of those consciousnesses" without mentioning "relying on matter," [it would be unclear].
Faith is also pure;

it should therefore be called "the eye" and so forth. If one speaks only of that consciousness perceiving form without mentioning its reliance on purity, then all eleven kinds of form would be collectively termed "form."
All [the sense organs] should be designated as "eye" and so forth; if one speaks only of that consciousness's reliance on the pure [organ] without mentioning "matter" (rūpa),
it is clear that this refers to its purity,
and that its substance is not the basis [of the consciousness].
If one were to take consciousness as the basis [for the compound], it would be possible to interpret it as a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound;
in order to preclude this interpretation, the word "form" (*rūpa*) is placed [at the beginning] to show that it is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound.
Therefore, the *Nyāyabindu* states:
"An explanation such as this is intended to dispel doubts and difficulties."
One must set aside the term "form" (rūpa).
If one speaks of consciousness as being "dependent," according to the possessive compound (bahuvrīhi), then pure faith would have to be the eye and other sense faculties.
Therefore, the term "form" (rūpa) is established in order to exclude this interpretation.
There is not a single dharma that, while having consciousness as its support, is pure such that it could be explained in this way.

Therefore, the term "matter" (rūpa) is extremely useful; as stated in the treatise above, if one were to say only that "that consciousness relies on matter" without mentioning "purity," then the four objects that support the sense organs would also be called "bases."

Furthermore, it would also be designated as "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) and should be named after the eye and so forth. If one were to speak only of that consciousness as "pure matter" (rūpaprasāda) without mentioning its basis,
[it would be incorrect].
A clear pond or a bright mirror are also pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) and should therefore be called "eye" and so forth.

If one were to speak fully, there would be no error in designating them as such based on pure matter in the three directions. However, if one speaks only of "relying on pure matter" without mentioning that consciousness, [the definition remains incomplete].
The five [bases] should be treated identically.

Since it is shown that there are five distinct differences among the faculties such as the eye, they are referred to as "those consciousnesses. If one were to speak only of "those consciousnesses" without mentioning their reliance on translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*), then the five consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and so forth—would have to be named simply after the eye and so on. Alternatively, this may be the case.
In this context, it should be stated that it is the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) which serves as the support for that consciousness.
If one were to speak only of "support" (*āśraya*) without specifying "that which is supported" (*āśrita*),
it would be confused with the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
The body, in relation to the four consciousnesses,
is also a translucent material form (*rūpaprasāda*) that serves as a support (*āśraya*),
yet it is not the fundamental basis (*āśraya*).
Therefore, the verse relies on words to manifest that which is based upon them.
The Commentary states, "up to this extensive explanation," referring to the word "that" (*tat*) in the verse.
There are two interpretations of this passage;
this is the first interpretation.
Regarding the phrase "that [person]":
Regarding those objects such as form:
since the five groups of consciousness take those five objects as their conditions,
they are referred to as "those consciousnesses."
The translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serves as the basis for that consciousness is called the faculty (*indriya*).
This citation from scripture intends to prove that the faculty is translucent matter.
Alternatively, the phrase "or again, 'that'... refers to the full exposition [of the faculties] as previously stated.
The second explanation clarifies that term:
"that" refers to those very faculties;
that upon which consciousness relies is called the eye and so forth.
The treatise says, "eye-consciousness,
etc.," clearly showing that those [terms] refer to the faculties and not the objects.
Having already explained the five faculties, the five objects are now explained next.

The verse states: "That which reaches [the sense organ] and contact have eleven as their nature.
This verse provides the answer. All verses composed in India follow the rules of grammatical phonology (*śabda-vidyā*).

if flavor comes first and fragrance later, it does not constitute such a violation.
Now, following the original translation, flavor precedes fragrance. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
The reason for explaining them out of order is to demonstrate that the arising of those objects and consciousnesses lacks fixed sequence;
that is to say, when those five consciousnesses arise, their order is not fixed.
The Commentary states: "Up to 'improper [action] as the last'.
Within the prose section, this constitutes one interpretation of the five sense objects.
Second, the general and specific explanations of the arising of consciousness.
Below this, the five objects are explained;
the text consists of five parts. First: "That which is seen is called form (*rūpa*)."
Regarding the explanation within the objective sphere of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the substance of form;
second, the analysis of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*). Within the presentation of the substance of form, there are three general explanations.
This is the first explanation of the verse regarding the two types of matter (*rūpa*): first, color (*varṇa*);
second, shape (*saṃsthāna*). There are four colors:
blue, yellow, red, and white.

This is the primary manifest color; the other eight types of manifest colors—light, shadow, brightness, darkness, clouds, smoke, dust, and mist—are established as differentiations of these four basic colors. Light is subsumed under yellow.
When the sun first rises, that which appears red is due to the reflection of other objects;

alternatively, the light may be subsumed under the category of red, or the light may be subsumed under the categories of yellow and red. Shadow and darkness are subsumed under the category of blue-black. Luminosity is generally subsumed under the categories of blue, yellow, red, and white.

Because they all possess luminosity; clouds, smoke, dust, and mist are all subsumed within the categories of blue, yellow, red, and white. Question: Are light and the other seven colors merely four distinct varieties?
Is it not perhaps that these are merely provisional?
The commentary explains: if one considers their fundamental nature, they consist only of the four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white.
Based on the distinctions of meaning within these four, the remaining eight names are established.
Each has its own substantial entity and is not merely nominal. Question:

If clouds, smoke, dust, and mist are subsumed under visible color (*varṇa*), how are they included within the "both" category among the four alternatives? One explanation states: clouds, smoke, dust, and mist are visible color and not shape (*saṃsthāna*).
That which makes its characteristics manifest is called "manifest" (*vijñapti*).
That which possesses substantial resistance and is coarse and prominent, such that it can be known through touch,
is described as "shape" (*saṃsthāna*), such as long, short, and so forth.
Clouds, smoke, dust, and mist lack this obstructive function;
therefore, it is revealed that [the object] is not material.
This constitutes a logical proof.
Furthermore, in various treatises,
it is stated that among the four types— clouds and so forth— both shape (*saṃsthāna*) and color (*varṇa*) are subsumed under manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*).
If they also pertain to shape, why are they not so described?
This is the scriptural evidence.
However, when various treatises state that the four types, such as clouds and so forth, are subsumed under the category of "concurrent phrases" (*jugu*),
it means that these four kinds of color are not actually [inherently] long and so on.
It appears as long and so forth;
because the mental consciousness relies on the power of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) toward that [object], it gives rise to the cognition of length and so forth,
just as in the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Although they take actual physical form as their object,
through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one forms the perception of it as a livid corpse and so forth;
by means of these four colors.
Since the explanations of "manifest," "somewhat coarse," "growing," and so forth are included within the [respective] categories,
they are subsumed under the same clauses as shadow, light, radiance, and darkness.
Existing in space, its own substance is dispersed;
it manifests only by relying upon a material basis.
Because it is subtle, it is not the same as clouds and the like. A second interpretation states:
Clouds, smoke, dust, and mist encompass both visible color (*varṇa*) and shape (*saṃsthāna*).
This is because all treatises state that they are subsumed under the category of "both.
Nevertheless, within those same treatises, it is stated that these four—clouds and so forth—are included within visible color.

Because their arising and manifestation are characterized by the strength of wisdom, both are manifested and subsumed. Question: If, according to the strength of their arising and manifestation, they are thus manifested and subsumed, then in the fourfold classification (catuṣkoṭi), they should be included in the first alternative.
How is it that these are subsumed under the "conjunction" (ubhaya-pada)?
The explanation states:
among the four propositions, the first two are single propositions.
Although this is explained forcefully based on the arising of cognition,
if there were distinct new arisings of shape or color within this aggregate,
two simple propositions would be established.
Although the four colors such as clouds manifest with distinct shapes,
there is no separate new manifestation [of color] produced; since shape arises simultaneously [with color],
it is not at all surprising that cognition [of shape] arises.
Therefore, it is not included in the first category. The third explanation states:
clouds, smoke, dust, and mist are included within the category of visible color (*varṇa*).
This is the same as the first interpretation.
However, the statement regarding the "concurrent phrase" (ubhayakoṭi) represents the view of other masters. The fourth interpretation states:
Clouds, smoke, dust, and mist—
whether manifesting as pervasive phenomena or as distinct forms— are explained in the same manner as the second interpretation.
However, the statement that "manifest" refers to the view of other masters.
Regarding the phrase "or twenty, up to shadow, light, brightness, and darkness":
this is the second explanation of form as being either twentyfold.
This differs from the previous explanation in its expansion and contraction,
yet there is no contradiction.
[The colors are] blue, yellow, red, and white.

It can be known through direct perception that when one speaks of "long" and "short," the atoms of length and the atoms of shortness each possess their own distinct substance and exist in a state of mutual intermingling.
That which is long appears short;

that which is short appears long. Question: If length, shortness, and so forth each possess distinct atoms (*paramāṇu*), why does the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 136, state: [as follows]?
One should know that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the most subtle form of matter;
it is not long, short, square, round, or the like.
The commentary explains:
The *Vibhāṣā* relies on a single atom (*paramāṇu*) as the ultimate,
most subtle division that can no longer be divided;
it is not visible to the eye and is said to lack dimensions such as length and so forth.
This treatise is based on the observation that, once [the entity] has passed away,
there exists a category of substantial reality,
because it grows and so forth.
Therefore, they are called "long" and so forth.
If one explains length in a general sense, both shortness and length may be either conventional (prajñapti) or substantial (dravya).
This applies when length and shortness are considered in relation to one another among the twenty kinds of form.
To compare the real with the real;
if one generally compares length and shortness by means of various provisional aggregates,
then one is comparing the provisional with the provisional.
Therefore, in the ninth fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā*, while explaining the various types of existence (*bhava*),
the third master states:
"The fifth is relative existence (*apekṣā-sat*)."
This refers to matters such as the length and shortness of this shore and that shore. Furthermore,
it is explained that what can be measured is called "long," while that which cannot be measured is called "short."
Regarding those things in the world that are said to be short in shape:

they are conventionally designated as "short" within that which is long, just as one conventionally designates something as "light" within that which is heavy. Question: Since these subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of shortness are already numerous...
How can it be said that they are immeasurable?
Although their manifestations are manifold,
they remain immeasurable.
Just as extremely subtle atoms (paramāṇu), though they exist in great numbers,
cannot be weighed, so too extremely short [atoms], though numerous, [cannot be measured].
Yet it is immeasurable.
If one says that what is seen by the eye is not measurable,
then visibility (ābhāsvara) is also seen by the eye.
It ought to be measurable.
If you say that because they are gathered together they should be measurable,
then fragrance and so forth, being likewise gathered together, should also be measurable.
Since these are mixed together and cannot be measured, so too the mixture of short and long cannot be measured.

"Square" refers to the directions of the realm; "round" refers to being circular; that which is convex in the center is called "high"; that which is concave in the center is called "low. Question: What is the distinction between "long" and "high"?
What distinguishes "short" from "low"?
The explanation states:
"long" and "short" are measured according to the four sides.
High and low are based on the middle.
However, when people of the world speak of these things as "high" or "low," they are speaking of high and low within the context of long and short; thus it is explained.
Length and shortness are determined by the horizontal;
height and depth are measured by the vertical.
It is in common worldly parlance that the vertical is termed "long" or "short."
Because "long" and "short" are spoken of in relation to high and low; "cloud" is the name for the vapor of dragons;
"smoke" is the name for the vapor of fire; "dust" is the name for fine soil blown by the wind;
other colors are explained as in the text itself. Question: Regarding the twenty kinds of color within the category of reflected color (*pratibimba-rūpa*).
By what category of color is it subsumed?
The explanation says:
it is subsumed under manifest color (*varṇa*), not shape (*saṃsthāna*).
Now, as for form and color,
they must necessarily depend on ultimate resistance (*pratigha*) to manifest that they possess physical form;
such is the case with images in mirrors and the like.
Tactile sensation cannot discern it;
it is like a shadow and so forth.
Therefore, it is not a shape.
As for what is called "seeing a form," it resembles a form but is not real;
it is like the fire in a mirror, which resembles fire but is not true fire.
Among the primary colors (*varṇa*), as appropriate, it is comprised within the four colors: blue, yellow, red, and white.
It is taught that the "likeness" (*pratibimba*) is a primary color and not a shape (*saṃsthāna*).
This is explained in detail as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Logic),
fascicle 34. The reason we know that it is not any other kind of manifest color is that wherever there is light, there can be no shadow.
Because an image appears within the light, the image is not a reflection.

The detailed explanation that the image is not a reflection is as extensive as in the *Nyāyānusāra*. Although there is no extant text stating that the image is not something else manifest, [it is so].
This can be understood by analogy with a reflection.
Since the image appears within the light,
it indicates that the image is not a shadow.
From this it may be inferred that the image appears within the light,
indicating that the image is not in darkness;
since the image appears within the light...
The image is neither shadow nor darkness;
by analogy, it should be understood that the image appears within the shadow.
The image is neither light; if one were to say that the image appearing within light is subsumed by the light itself, [that would be incorrect].
To claim that the appearance of an image within a shadow is subsumed by the shadow is also illogical;
for what is called "light" is the solar radiance,
and it is not the solar radiance itself.
That which obstructs the arising of light is called a shadow;
it is not produced by an obstruction. Clouds, smoke, dust, and mist are both manifest and possess shape.
Principle is not image-form,
because image-form is not shape. Some say:
The claim that clouds and the like are manifest colors (varṇa) is not a definitive proof;
furthermore, it is logically impossible for them to be reflections in the sky.
Other masters say that this [discussion] extends up to the twenty-first [chapter].
The third section describes alternative explanations:
it states that in the space on each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru,
there is a distinct color.
It is called the "single manifest color of space.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Following Reasoning), fascicle 34, states:
"The single manifest color of space."
That is to say, one sees the pure color appearing in the sky upon Mount Sumeru. Question: What constitutes the essence of this single manifest color of space?
Answer: It has the color of the space-element (ākāśa-dhātu) as its essence.
Therefore, the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Right Reasoning),
chapter one, states: "Some say that there are twenty-one types of form (*rūpa*),
with the color of space being the twenty-first."
This is precisely the differentiation of color within the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*). Question:
If its essence consists of the color of the element of space, why does the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*, chapter eleven, state:
"The single manifest color of space is just like blue, yellow, red, and white"?
According to that treatise,
it takes blue, yellow, red, and white as its substance.
The commentary explains:
That treatise states: "As for those [colors]— blue, yellow, red, and white—
it means that each of these colors appears individually in the sky on each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru."
It is called the matter of the space element (*ākāśadhātu-rūpa*).
The word "like" (*yathā*) means "resembling.
This is the single manifest color of space.
It resembles blue, yellow, red, or white, yet it is not identical to them;
this may be so. Or perhaps the word "like" (ru) means "is" (shi).
This single manifestation of color as space is precisely that which is blue, yellow, red, and white. According to various treatises,
this is the color of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Since its substance consists of shadow, light, brightness, and darkness,
how can it be described as blue, yellow, red, and white?
The explanation says:
Blue, yellow, red, and white have two categories:
if they are the very substance of blue and so forth,
they are not the color of the space element.
If the blue and other colors that appear on the four sides of Mount Sumeru, distinct from its substance,
are also the color of the space-element (ākāśadhātu),
another interpretation holds that although this color of the space-element has light, shadow, brilliance, and darkness as its essence.
However, as for those [colors]— light, shadow, brightness, and darkness—
if they are considered according to their actual manifestation,
they are also included within blue, yellow, red, and white, as appropriate.
Therefore, the Nyāyabindu states:
"The four kinds, such as blue and so forth,
are primary manifest colors."
The eight kinds, beginning with clouds, are its specific classifications. Regarding the above treatise: if one speaks of blue and so forth, it is explained according to the fundamental;
if one speaks of light and so forth, it is discussed according to the derivative.
Each is established according to its own specific meaning, and they do not contradict one another. Question:
Is the single manifest color of space the same as the matter of the space-element (ākāśa-dhātu)?
The matter of the space-element consists of light, shadow, clarity, and darkness.
It is not yet known:
among shadows, light, radiance, and darkness, what constitutes the substance of the single manifest color of space?
The commentary states:
If one refers to all matter within the realm of space,
it takes light, shadow, brightness, and darkness as its substance.
If one relies on their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
the four types of form are not fixed; herein,
it is stated that the single manifest color of space is the form of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
This form of the space-element has luminosity as its essence.
The body of Mount Sumeru is composed of four precious substances;
these jewels appear within the sky.
This refers to luminous color.
Therefore, various treatises state that "jewel-flame" (ratnārcis) is named "luminosity" (āloka).
For this reason, it is known that [the sun] is not light, shadow, or darkness;
the radiance of the sun is called "light."
Since it is not the solar radiance itself, it is not light;
rather, it is the obstruction of light that causes luminosity to arise.
Within this, the visibility of other forms is called "shadow."
The opposite of this is darkness.
It is not a shadow because it does not arise from an obstruction;
it is not darkness because one perceives forms within it.
Based on this reasoning and evidence, it is certain that this is light;
therefore, these luminous colors are precisely the distinctions of blue, yellow, red, and white.
If one explains it in this way:
Space is a single manifest color (*varṇa*).
This does not contradict the correct doctrine taught by other masters;
however, it is explained separately in order to clarify its distinction [from other colors].
Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Scroll One.
